The Redemption of Night City (With Cavéats) I’ve been here since the beginning, and while Cyberpunk 2077 will be studied as a remarkable turnaround, we shouldn't forget that it launched two years too early. CD Projekt Red arguably got a "free pass" for a state they knew wasn't ready, but the current version of the game is finally something remarkable. The Good The World: Night City is visually outstanding. It is easily one of the most detailed environments ever put in a game, and it’s easy to get lost in the atmosphere. Build Variety: Spec-ing your character is a total joy. The game truly allows you to play how you want, making it incredibly approachable regardless of your preferred playstyle. Masterful Side Quests: Some of the darker, gloomier side stories are the best parts of the game. They are masterfully written and stand as great stories in their own right. Combat: Whether you're hacking or shooting, the combat loop is genuinely fun. The Bad The Writing: While the characters are mostly great, the dialogue can often be "cringe." V feels somewhat bland as a protagonist, and the character creation system still feels like it lacks meaningful impact. Navigation: As beautiful as the map is, it just isn’t fun to navigate. Its scale is impressive, but getting from point A to point B often feels like a chore. The "Arasaka" Irony: There is a lot of deserved love for the game now, but let's not forget the corporate decisions behind the launch. In the end, CDPR acted a lot like the megacorps they satirize. Verdict It’s not a solid 5/5, but the story and the sheer detail of the world keep me coming back. It is a must-play for the atmosphere alone, even if the "soul" of the protagonist and the dialogue occasionally miss the mark

review_text: TLDR: This is a great game but a weak RPG. Cyberpunk’s incredible narrative, enhanced by its DLC, is undoubtedly worth playing, or at least trying. There’s a lot to say about this game’s launch and subsequent redemption, but from someone who played it through multiple endings before 2.0, most of the best parts of the game were always there, if not just more accessible now. The story is great, tense and complex with interesting characters that pulls you along all the while you as V build your rep by taking on fun, if not short, gigs throughout Night City. There’s some tastes of meaningful choice in the main story (and moreso in the DLC) but outside of that there’s little room for you to actually express yourself in this world, especially with how predetermined some aspects of your character are. Even basic features of expression like clothing, looks, and vehicles are seriously limited by a lot of modern RPG standards. More than that, one playthrough of the game’s main narratives will lead you through most of the game’s side content, with about 5 non-repeatable hours of “postgame content” (exclusively in the DLC). Sure, there’s always the other endings, but after that what are you left with? With how full Night City is I’m shocked by how dead the moment to moment exploration is. Night City is crowded, but hardly alive. It may be heretical to say, but outside of CD Projekt’s incredible curated content the transitory gameplay could be swapped with Starfield’s exploration. Its still well worth the money, ESPECIALLY recommended on sale, and mods can fill some of that empty space I’m dissatisfied with, but every so often I’ll stare wistfully at its icon before jumping in just to look at a cleared map and log out.

The story, while it explores tropes that are typical to this genre - it does it quite well. Colorful (maybe too much during daytime) yet dark, near altfuture, urban dystopia. Sadly this whole immersive experience can be broken by the bugs that persisted in this game over the years. You can spot civilians phasing through walls, multiple car models being stuck on top of or inside each other, enemies shooting you through some walls, animations/scripted events not playing correctly or at all. One of the more annoying bugs that I remember from when I first played the game ~5 years ago was "clown boots" - the game loops the sound of the crushing bottles as your footsteps when you first walk on them in specific area during the Evelyn questline and it doesn't stop unless you restart the game... 9.5/10 TL;DR: A beautifully crafted open world with exceptional combat variety and style along with environments that are bound to leave you startstruck. However, obscure NPC questlines and lack of in-game tracking can make for a frustrating time without external tools if you are looking to explore all. Detailed Review: Pros: - Boss fights feel like an intricate dance, with clear punish windows while still subverting expectations on subsequent attempts with their delayed or unpredictable attacks. - Excellent build diversity, especially hybrid/quality builds like Faith-Arcane or Strength-Intelligence. - Stunning, vast landscapes that encourage exploration due to the mystique they carry. - Dungeons are generally well-designed, with occasional unique gimmicks that break monotony and keep it fresh. Cons: - NPC questlines are rather obscure and difficult to follow organically. - No in-game checklist or tracking for collected items, making completionist runs unnecessarily reliant on external tools like MapGenie (Scadutree Fragments I'm looking at you). - Just like any other FromSoftware game, ELDEN RING also doesn't explain much about its mechanics making it difficult to recommend to a lot of casual players. Shadow of the Erdtree DLC: A very vertical and puzzle like map layout makes it very interesting but also frustrating to navigate the Land of Shadows. The performance is overall worse compared to the base game and a lot of bosses like to do attacks which are too long (almost like cutscenes). Despite all of that, the beautiful landscapes, more weapon variety and a good story made it quite engaging for me.

The sound design elevates that sense of place even further—haunting ambient tracks, thunderous boss themes, and crisp combat audio all work together to pull you deeper into the Lands Between. The combat is where everything really came together for me. It’s challenging, sometimes brutally so, but it’s also deliberate, responsive, and endlessly rewarding once the rhythm sets in. What made the difficulty feel more manageable this time was embracing both player summons and spirit ashes. They don’t trivialize the game, but they smooth out the rough edges enough to let the brilliance of the encounters shine through instead of feeling like a wall. After finally “getting it,” I can confidently say Elden Ring is an exceptional experience—one that rewards persistence with moments of awe, triumph, and discovery. 9.5/10.

Where do I begin? By the time I was done with it, the game left me completely disappointed. Most of the negative reviews have captured all the significant problems with this game so I'll keep it (relatively) short. My favorite games in the Fromsoft catalogue are Dark Souls and Sekiro (also among my favorite games of all time). These games feel deliberately designed; Dark Souls made you feel like exploring a dangerous land, and Sekiro's combat system is truly one of a kind. But Elden Ring? It's a video game ass video game. Everything in this game exists for the player's benefit. Side dungeons almost always end in boss fights with a treasure chest to reward the player. Stakes of Marika make it convenient to fight bosses. Sites of Grace abound so that you never feel the tension of exploration (also free fast travel). Every single death in this game will only be due to bosses, or sometimes gravity. Don't wanna fight overworld enemies? Get on Torrent and ride away. The open world is simply a collection of all the dungeons they made spread horizontally. Is the open world truly open then? Nope, there's a strictly linear progression with some side stuff along the way, with arbitrary progression gates like Morgott's Seal and Great rune requirements. Balance is literally non-existent. Is the combat good then? It's basically Dark Souls combat again. There's a gazillion weapons, but they all mostly play the same, you know how it is. Boss fights are now true shonen anime style affairs, wait for your turn and dodge while the boss does his wombo combo and then poke. Repeat all over again for a 100 bosses, and the nail in the coffin is that a significant portion of them are repeats. Not even remembrance bosses are spared. Don't even get me started on the DLC. I was genuinely excited to play this game, and sadly, this made me question the future of Soulslikes from Fromsoft. I guess we'll have to wait and see.

It works well when it does, but enemy design quite often draws it back. On the bright side, there's a hand cannon. And crossbows are finally functional. Open-world nature of this game clashes violently with its DS1-style quest structure - so if you meet a character you think has a quest, read online where to meet them next. But then there's lore, and aesthetic, and all the actually good areas (though those start rather late).

review_text: 5/5 stars Elden Ring is special. I feel like FromSoft has been building up to this game since the first release of Dark Souls, possibly longer. This game is extremely well made and stunning in every sense of the word. I can talk about how beautiful the world is, how amazing the story is, how fine tuned and gratifying the combat is, how much fun it is to explore but I know you have heard that all before. As someone who has played DS1, DS3 and Bloodborne I am used to some of the basic knowledge of how these games work. It is tricky though, because this game falls victim to one of the sharpest learning curves out there. It is difficult to call this a negative because I feel that this is part of what makes this game so special. I am a firm believer that this game would not work in a world without the internet. I feel like the meta of searching how to do some niche thing and finding an entire community of passionate people enjoying the game is part of the experience itself. Talking with your friends who have played it and explaining different tactics, gear, secrets and more is part of the fun. This game is not friendly, and I am not referring to the fact that it is "hard", but that it intentionally does not guide the player in any way. Yes there is a tutorial but most of the games mechanics are not explained in any way and just left for the players to experiment and find themselves. I spent my first 30 hours in the game when it first came out not understanding how Ashes of War worked. Not until I picked the game up again and started over recently did I start to understand how the combat worked fully. I think the best example of this is the story of Elden Ring itself. A player can play hundreds of hours of the game and not understand a single thing of what's going on. Not understanding what NPCs are talking about, not understanding the overarching plot, maybe they dont even understand who Michela is (the key character in the story). Not until I started watching lore videos did I start piecing everything together and start to appreciate the impact someone like George RR Martin had on the creation of this game. Everything is not there to serve you, it just is. I think this is kind of magical in a way, breathing a sense of life into the world, as if it has always been there and you are just a passerby of this breathing beautiful world. This is how all of the mechanics in the game feel, from the exploration to the combat to the obtuse side quests. Its tricky because if it was executed in any other way I would say this is just bad design but I believe it is the intentional fun of it. They want you to research, they want you to learn. By the time you finish Elden Ring for the first time, if you start all over from a new save you will undoubtedly be a better player because you have taken the time to learn and understand how the game works, not just because your end game character is level 150+. This game is not for the causal player, and I am not saying that to gatekeep, I am saying that because I don't think you will be able to enjoy Elden Ring in any casual way, you absolutely have to “lock in”. It's funny to see when people are in the middle of their first playthrough because I have seen it basically take over their consciousness, once it starts, it works its way into your brain and it's hard to not stop thinking about it. I know that happened to me. If you are willing to give Elden Ring your time and energy, you will not regret it. It is absolutely fantastic.

[u]An absolute must‑play within the FromSoftware lineage.[/u] Elden Ring takes the studio’s signature challenge‑driven design and expands it into a sweeping open world that feels endlessly explorable. While it departs from the tightly structured progression of Dark Souls 1–3 (a format I personally prefer) the shift still brings a unique strength. The Lands Between evoke the same sense of boundless possibility that made Skyrim so iconic, rewarding curiosity with challenging encounters, layered storytelling, and a level of discovery rarely matched in modern RPGs. However, this sense of discovery didn't come without drawbacks. The sheer freedom of pathing makes FromSoftware’s already cryptic questlines even harder to track, often to the point of feeling overwhelming. NPC arcs can become fragmented or unintentionally skipped, and the open structure occasionally disrupts the narrative flow, creating moments where major story beats feel out of order or disconnected from the intended progression. Regarding the graphics, it’s impossible not to highlight the sheer beauty of the world FromSoftware has crafted. Every vista, dungeon, and battlefield feels meticulously composed, often looking more like art then the video games of past. Whether standing still to admire the horizon or caught in the chaos of combat, nearly every moment feels screenshot-worthy. It’s a visually astonishing experience that elevates the sense of wonder throughout the journey.

Elden Ring stands as a seminal achievement in interactive myth-making. One thing this game does is encourage an approach to character progression. Whether you prefer the visceral, heavy-hitting cadence of a colossal sword or the distance of glintstone sorceries, the mechanical framework is amazing. The game really shines when you start experimenting with making hybrid builds, like mixing stats like Strength and Faith or Dexterity and Arcane to create a build that feels entirely personal. The lore is this game is really mind-blowing as it doesn't just hand you a plot, it sort of force you to piece together a tragic mystery of a broken world. As a "tarnished" which is sent into the world long after signifcant events occur, witnessing the aftermath of a war that fractured reality itself and creating a narrative depth it make the game feel both haunting and monumental. A game that truly earns its title of GOTY and will undoubtedly remain a cherished masterpiece for many.

The art team did something special here. Exploration is rewarded on such a minute level - every corner or ledge or alternate path rewards something major, it's impressive a game of this scope can deliver surprises consistently. Towards the end, when you get to the snowy area you're somewhat grateful the later zones are a little smaller and less content-dense. Combat, once you get used to the rules, is a fun dance of swing and dodge timings, and never gets stale. Towards the end you start deleting everything pretty quickly but even the later zones' trash mobs are not to be trifled with. You can cheese pretty much any encounter if you wish - you'll get there anyway once you've spent enough runes and points on leveling. Game is GOATed for a reason, no cap.

Elden Ring is a massive achievement, but the difficulty sometimes feels like its coming from the wrong place. After putting in over 100 hours, I have a few thoughts. The Good: World & Play The level design is genuinely amazing. The way the world is built is top-tier; these levels are expansive, twisting, and turning into each other in ways that are actually hard to wrap your head around. It’s beautiful to look at, and the enemy variety is awesome. The 'come up' of getting stronger is where it really shines. The Bad: Controls & "Artificial" Difficulty I found the controls to be ridiculous, I don't think making a game harder with cumbersome controls is good design. The queue up system for inputs acts so strange that I found myself still making mistakes even after 100+ hours. The amount of times I have accidently dismounted from my horse its unbelievable, call me bad, but this is my experience. Bad physics isn't a puzzle, it's just frustrating. Same goes for some of the site of grace layouts; tedious for no real gain. The Ugly: Narrative & Inventory The story makes very little sense. Call me a smooth brain, but FromSoft just doesn't tell a good story I almost never knew what I was actually doing.. The lack of explanation carries over to items, I have a million things in my inventory, most of which where useless, or that I had no idea how to use. Managing it all was a chore; when the expansion started I had to look up what the first item did. Why? Multiplayer: PVP & Coop The PVP was mostly try hards wasting my time, the native coop is quite clucky and I highly recommend Seamless Co-op mod, it made the experience a lot better for me. It removes a ton of the friction from cooperative play. Performance: My PC is a literal god computer, and I’m still seeing 40 FPS at times. Lul. Final Take: Its a gorgeous, expansive world with fun boss fights, and great multiplayer held back by clunky UI and controls. I still recommend it, its a fun game, but its probably going to piss you off at times.

review_text: This game is the absolute manifestation of perfection in gaming. As a fairly new player to the souls-like genre, I was worried initially. Not that I wouldn't like the game, I was rather worried about mechanical confusion. I was worried about the fact that I couldn't understand the game. This primarily stems from the fact that the lack of guidance can be problematic. That doesn't mean I want the game to literally take me by my hand and lead me to the ending, but complete lack of guidance makes the game less enjoyable for me. Elden Ring balances this perfectly. Yes, there were some things that required research, mainly new mechanics, but the guidance is firm and telling enough to give me breathing space. The game clearly tells you "go in that direction, and you will progress in some way", and then hints at what is optional. Its not written anywhere clearly, like in a quest log, but there are subtle and simple ways of guiding you that do not spoil you the game. Something that should also be noted is the method of storytelling. I had to learn this externally, but the game does not "tell a story" through collectibles, which is boring. The game tells a story by the environment. Almost everything in this game has a reason for its location, appearance, and behavior. Bosses tend resemble their personalities in the way they move, attack, speak, everything. The environment is shaped in such ways to tell a story. An NPC being concealed doesn't have to be just a visual decision, it can resemble something deeper and important. Not a lot of games take it to such a depth and often things looks the way "just because they were designed that way". A knight can have a very consistent pattern of attacking that does not change, because it literally "keeps calm". A teacher can test you, be consistent, and incredibly calm, but then once you fight his "real self", he throws away the composure, and becomes much more violent and desperate. The game does not have a perfectly linear gameplay, but it does not fail at "telling where is the main progress" either. if a fight feels too hard, you should come back later once you are stronger. Or you can switch up your strategy and lure the enemy somewhere. Weapons are not perfectly universal, and tend to have specific uses for specific situations. So holding onto one single weapon is not very ideal here, because experimenting is rewarded. A common complaint I see is the difficulty of this game. And I agree this game is difficult, but there is also a clear distinction between "difficult, because RNG", and "difficult, because of complex mechanics". there are games that are difficult only because of RNG, meaning you barely control the outcomes, the random elements do instead. These games tend to be much more frustrating, because you can learn only a very limited range of things, because there is so much outside of your control. But here? The game is not difficult, because of a ton of elements that you basically cannot control. The game is difficult, because of mechanical complexity. Bossfights, for example, are difficult, because you need to learn patterns. Learn patterns, recovery windows, read the enemy movement, tune your equipment,... Each death that happens has a clear reason. If you happen to die, you always know why and what killed you. The visual clarity is strong enough that you notice it and physically see it. This is the type of difficulty that is much less random and actually is fair. A boss can be extreme hard, but still can be extremely fun, even if you repeatedly die over and over. You never have to deal with the boss being extremely random and unpredictable. This is the closes to a skill-based game you can ever get. Yes, there are downsides. Especially in the engine. The game is obviously meant to be played with a controller, and on a console. That does not mean its unplayable on a keyboard, I would say the experience is pretty okay, but some keybinds can feel weird, and you may need to change them. The game is also permanently locked at 60fps, so your 1000hz monitor is useless here. And while unlocking it is possible, it can have some unpredictable outcomes, like some animations breaking, or acting weirdly. Not to mention that the engine is not really suited to hyper-optimize games. Foliage can be an issue, mainly around forests and trees. It can lower your fps on high settings, despite having capable hardware. I would also enjoy a bit better explanations of some systems. Not to necessarily add new explanations to gameplay mechanics, but to rather make the existing ones more clear and understandable. In the end I would say that the game is absolutely amazing. Its not often that I get so excited from games, and this one really made me enjoy gaming the same way when I was a young kid completely new to gaming. The price is a little high with small sales, but I would say its definitely worth it!

Absolute masterpiece. In my opinion, the game feels and looks better then Forza Horizon 4. The only games that look better or are on par with Forza Horizon 5 is something like Ready or Not (one of the only good UE5 titles where the devs actually cared for its artstyle and AMAZING performance, which is unbelievable to be said about UE5 titles), the upcoming GTA 6 and RDR2. AMAZING realism on the cars' engine sounds,(stuff like the Jesko and a few others can be improved, but still pretty good) the engine sounds of the vehicles are outstanding, so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ realistic. The hate the game got at launch wasn't really deserved, even though the launch wasn't the best, It has gotten much better now. The vehicle physics are also really great, not THAT realistic, but more arcadey. In this aspect, unlike the graphics, I think that the game being less realistic in vehicle physics is way more fun and adds onto the charm of the game instead of it being super realistic. The vehicle physics have realism, but not that much, I personally think it's perfect. PERFORMANCE IS ABSOLUTELY MINDBLOWING, a game made in 2021 that looks THIS GOOD and performs this AMAZINGLY is too good to be true, I average 90-105 FPS on High Settings with 8x MSAA (the MSAA implementation on this game is very good btw, doesnt look like a blurry mess on 1080p like how TAA and FXAA do, while performing better then them somehow in this game specifically) and sometimes see rare dips to 70-80 FPS, really playable, no studders even with a HDD! (I'm running the game on my 1TB 5400 RPM hard drive, and see no issues besides loading times), and my gaming laptop with an i7 10750H and a 3050 TI Laptop GPU (4gb vram) see no issues whatsoever! The story is also really great for an arcade racing game, had a LOT of fun on it and teaches you stuff regarding how racing is made to be fun, not to take it seriously. The DLCs, Playlists and events are also really well done. The Hot Wheels and Rally Adventure DLCs are very well done and had a lot of fun playing them! The Playlists feature is also pretty smart, it lets me get my favorite dream vehicles i want like the recent Mercedes AMG E63 S which was put on the last few playlists was one of my dream cars that I really wanted, and the playlist feature finally made my dream come true! I also got a few Porsches i wanted from it. Events are pretty great too, even community ones! Absolutely reccomend, i bought this game at full price cuz i couldn't wait for a discount. Note that i also played the game on one of my friends' PCs, and because of how good the game was, i decided to purchase it on Steam at full price (premium edition). 10/10, would reccomend if you're into these games.

After spending around 177 hours in Forza Horizon 5, I can confidently say that it is one of the most engaging open-world racing games I have played. The map set in Mexico is vibrant, diverse, and full of life, offering deserts, jungles, beaches, and mountains that make every drive feel fresh. The graphics are impressive, with detailed environments and cars that look almost real, especially when weather effects or lighting change the atmosphere. The gameplay is accessible but still rewarding. Whether you enjoy drifting, racing on asphalt, going off-road, or simply exploring the world, the game gives you complete freedom. The large collection of cars and the tuning system add depth, letting players experiment with different builds and driving styles. This makes the experience fun even after many hours of play. However, the game also has a few weaknesses. After long sessions, some activities start to feel repetitive, and certain story missions lack impact. The formula does not innovate much compared to previous titles, so experienced players may notice familiar patterns. Even so, Forza Horizon 5 remains an excellent racing game. Its beautiful world, huge variety of cars, and relaxed but exciting gameplay make it worth playing for many hours. For me, it has been a memorable experience, and it still has plenty to offer even after 177 hours on the road.

Overview After 134 hours with Forza Horizon 5, it is clear this is a game that knows how to keep you hooked. It is smooth, polished, and easy to enjoy, but the longer you play, the more certain cracks start to show beneath the surface. Pros Visually Impressive World Mexico looks stunning. The environments are varied, from deserts and jungles to coastlines, and everything is detailed and well crafted. From a visual standpoint, it is hard to complain. Driving Feels Just Right The handling is where the game really shines. It is accessible without being boring, and whether you are racing seriously or just cruising, it feels consistently good. Massive Car Collection There is a huge range of vehicles to choose from. You are never really short on options, and experimenting with different builds keeps things interesting. Freedom in Gameplay You are not forced into anything. You can race, explore, tune, or just drive around. That flexibility makes it easy to pick up anytime. Long Lasting Appeal Even after 134 hours, it still has moments that pull you back in. The core gameplay loop is strong enough to hold attention over time. Cons World Feels Empty Over Time While the map looks beautiful, it can start to feel lifeless. Outside of events, there is not much happening dynamically, which makes long drives feel a bit hollow after a while. Repetitive Event Structure Many races and challenges start blending into each other. You notice the repetition more the longer you play. Weak Story Presence The story is minimal and forgettable. It does not add much to the overall experience. Online Inconsistencies Multiplayer is not always reliable. Connection issues and matchmaking problems can take away from the experience. AI Balance Issues The AI can feel uneven, either too easy or oddly difficult at times. Underwhelming Engine Sounds A noticeable drawback. Many cars lack distinct, powerful sound profiles, which takes away from the immersion, especially for a car focused game. Final Verdict Forza Horizon 5 gets the fundamentals right, driving, visuals, and accessibility, but it does not always maintain depth in the long run. It is a great game to jump into, but over time, the emptiness of the world and repetition start to stand out. Still, if you enjoy open world racing, it is worth experiencing.

After spending about 120 hours in Forza Horizon 5 and unlocking almost all of the achievements, I feel like I have experienced nearly everything the game has to offer. First of all, the game is visually stunning. The map based on Mexico is beautiful, the car selection is huge, and the driving physics are still some of the best in the arcade-racing genre. However, after a long time playing, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive. Many events begin to feel the same, and this is something that also reminds me of Forza Horizon 4. The core gameplay loop hasn’t changed much between the two games. The DLCs are a mixed experience. The Rally Adventure DLC is actually quite interesting. The rally mechanics, dirt roads, and more technical driving create a refreshing change of pace compared to the base game. It feels more focused and challenging, which I appreciated. On the other hand, the Hot Wheels DLC was less interesting for me. While the tracks look impressive and creative, the gameplay quickly becomes more about spectacle than driving skill, and the novelty wears off faster than expected. One mode that I personally didn’t enjoy is “The Eliminator”. While the idea of a battle-royale style racing mode is creative, in practice it often feels frustrating and somewhat random. Encounters can depend too much on luck, car drops, or map positioning rather than pure driving skill. Because of this, the mode never really felt satisfying or balanced to me, even though I appreciate the attempt to add something different. Another downside is the lack of a meaningful story. There are some narrative elements, but they are very light and mostly serve as short introductions to events. Compared to how big the game world is, the story content feels minimal. Overall, Forza Horizon 5 is still a very polished and enjoyable racing game, especially in the first dozens of hours. But after completing most of the achievements and spending over 120 hours in the game, the repetition and lack of deeper progression or story can make it feel a bit monotonous. Still, for fans of arcade racing and car collecting, it remains a solid experience.

review_text: Forza Horizon 5 feels like a [b]tech demo[/b]. [h2]the core and technical aspects[/h2] the core of the game - driving and racing the cars - is incredibly well done and has clearly had a lot of effort and time invested towards it over the course of the franchise's lifespan. the simcade engine is the best of its kind and no other competitor comes close. driving remains immensely satisfying irrespective of the type of vehicle you're maneuvering, the terrain surface you're on, or weather conditions you're under. the game consistently looks, sounds, and performs very well. [hr][/hr] but it ends there. it's as if the developers had invested a lot of time and care into creating an incredibly solid base for a racing game, but then skimped out on all the additional aspects that wouldn't have required nearly as much effort or resources, but that would've greatly contributed to the quality of the final product. that's where the tech demo analogy comes from. first case in point: [h2]the map[/h2] the team was clearly capable of creating a large, varied, beautiful, and functional open world map. Mexico certainly ticks all of those boxes, and more: the volcano, the jungles, the many long, winding and twisting roads with great verticality, the beach town, the stadium and test track - i could go on. [b]on paper it's perfect[/b]. i much prefer it to the predecessor's Edinburgh. but holy sh*t is it [b]empty[/b]. the NPC vehicle traffic is so incredibly sparse. there are [i]zero[/i] pedestrians, like, at all. there's no people. there's no proper intersections, no parking garages, no gas stations, no traffic lights. there's no [i]things happening[/i]. no airplanes in the sky, boats on water, no service vehicles, no wildlife (outside of howler monkeys? and some birds), no events. the one urban area in the game feels like a complete ghost town. it's embarrassing. it looks and feels completely fake. this has been the case throughout the entirety of the franchise's lifespan. The Crew perfected the open-world racing map in 2018. so why can't Forza Horizon? [h2]story[/h2] terrible and completely dispensable in every possible aspect. ninety five percent of the storylines revolve around you driving a vehicle from point A to point B on the map while some at best completely forgettable and at worst extremely annoying character yaps about some boring ♥♥♥♥ in an irritatingly fake and forced spanish accent with involuntary spansih lingo sprinkled in occasionally. it's all totally dry, inoffensive, and boring, with zero character, no emotion, and a total lack of any plot. just absolutely terrible. the only slightly redeemable aspect are some of the scripted "Showcase" events, which seem more like technical presentations rather than parts of the story. [h2]progression[/h2] there is none. the currency model is optimized... - for the 10 year old playing the game on the living room Xbox whose parents bought it for him at $80, and who certainly wouldn't appreciate driving a beat-down Ford for the first 10 hours of the game. and that's fine. but there has to be a fine line, a compromise? the game showers you with rewards at every possible step. you earn credits as a reward for completing races, showcases, and events - and cars (and their upgrades) [i]do[/i] cost credits - but that aspect very quickly becomes totally irrelevant as you're constantly rewarded with Wheelspins, which in turn give you credits and cars in extreme abundance. the new "Accolades" system is a diamond in the rough - a good idea in isolation, which ultimately suffers from being part of a larger, flawed system. the one aspect of progression that's done right is what the game aptly calls [i]Hard To Find[/i] cars - ones that cannot be purchased outright using credits nor won in a wheelspin. instead, they appear for limited time in either the [i]Forzathon Shop[/i] or as a reward in a seasonal Festival Playlist. and it is this limited nature and the FOMO associated with it is what makes you want to play the game and acquire the car, and what ultimately makes it that much more satisfying once you do. -- but even so it's hard to make these cars appear special or unique next to their cheap, readily available 150,000 CR supercar counterparts. so - if there's no story to follow or get invested into, and little feeling of progression as you play - what's left? [hr][/hr] well, it's not all bleak. again, the activities that benefit most from the game's great foundation are thankfully the ones you'll spend most of your time on - racing (whether against AI or online versus real opponents) and simply cruising around the map. and they're very polished, really enjoyable, and in my opinion enough to just barely overshadow all the negatives. at its core, Forza Horizon 5 is still very enjoyable. it just sucks that i can't help but keep wondering just how much better it would've been with a bit more effort.

review_text: Overview After 134 hours with Forza Horizon 5, it is clear this is a game that knows how to keep you hooked. It is smooth, polished, and easy to enjoy, but the longer you play, the more certain cracks start to show beneath the surface. Pros Visually Impressive World Mexico looks stunning. The environments are varied, from deserts and jungles to coastlines, and everything is detailed and well crafted. From a visual standpoint, it is hard to complain. Driving Feels Just Right The handling is where the game really shines. It is accessible without being boring, and whether you are racing seriously or just cruising, it feels consistently good. Massive Car Collection There is a huge range of vehicles to choose from. You are never really short on options, and experimenting with different builds keeps things interesting. Freedom in Gameplay You are not forced into anything. You can race, explore, tune, or just drive around. That flexibility makes it easy to pick up anytime. Long Lasting Appeal Even after 134 hours, it still has moments that pull you back in. The core gameplay loop is strong enough to hold attention over time. Cons World Feels Empty Over Time While the map looks beautiful, it can start to feel lifeless. Outside of events, there is not much happening dynamically, which makes long drives feel a bit hollow after a while. Repetitive Event Structure Many races and challenges start blending into each other. You notice the repetition more the longer you play. Weak Story Presence The story is minimal and forgettable. It does not add much to the overall experience. Online Inconsistencies Multiplayer is not always reliable. Connection issues and matchmaking problems can take away from the experience. AI Balance Issues The AI can feel uneven, either too easy or oddly difficult at times. Underwhelming Engine Sounds A noticeable drawback. Many cars lack distinct, powerful sound profiles, which takes away from the immersion, especially for a car focused game. Final Verdict Forza Horizon 5 gets the fundamentals right, driving, visuals, and accessibility, but it does not always maintain depth in the long run. It is a great game to jump into, but over time, the emptiness of the world and repetition start to stand out. Still, if you enjoy open world racing, it is worth experiencing.

Hades is a fun roguelike experience, where the player feels themselves becoming stronger and stronger after each attempt, leading to a strong sense of accomplishment. While at first slow and extremely challenging by experimenting with the wide variety of different weapons and boons (skills gained randomly in runs) the player will slower become more attuned to the combat within the game. It definitely feels very rewarding when you find a build that you can successfully beat runs with consistently by combining weapons skills and certain boons to make explosive combinations: the variety in this game is unreal as there are hundreds of different abilities to experiment with and combine together, but admittedly most of them are quite useless. My only gripe is that there are some issues when playing this game on deck, mainly some weirdly long loading times, especially when booting up the game. I have no idea why this happens and it my just be an issue I am experiencing.

In short: Hades is a great game and a mediocre Rogue-like. there are a lot of issues with the game, many of them addressed in the sequel. However, this is still a very good game and well worth your time. Really fun characters, That Supergiant writing quality and whit, and when its going well it feels electric, its just that most of the "Boons," the gifts from the Olympian gods that function as the modifiers for your runs, fluctuate between game warping and total dog water. in fact, there are more bad boons than good. You will have your favorite gods, and I suggest gravitating towards them and sticking to them, because my least favorite runs were the ones in which I tried to experiment or when I was trying to check off something for the list of prophecies that function as ways to gather resources for your upgrades. and the scarcity of resources for upgrades and the limited ways to accrue them is a whole other can of beans Should you play Hades? Yes. The Supergiant charm is here, the story of a troubled family is well written, but if you want a rogue-like you will sink your teeth in for countless hours? Maybe this will scratch some itch, but you can be better served elsewhere.

Besides very specific personal issues, (I don't like getting poison spammed by giant new york rats) This is perhaps one of THE best roguelite games I've ever played. It is insanely solid, the movement, combat, and replayability with difficulty modifiers is great, just great. You can practically slap together any build you want and can think of and it WILL work. The standard progression of Roguelites is in there, you get currency every run to use on upgrades and eventually you will feel like the demigod you are! The story is decent (if you already know Greek mythos, you know what happens in game, lol) and the music is stupid good. The characters are fun, the voice acting is great, and the humor (while sometimes not to my taste) is wonderfully done and it doesn't try too hard to make a joke happen which I appreciate. This game was SO good, it convinced me to buy the 2nd game! I would totally recommend anyone to give Hades a solid try. It is everything I want in a roguelite.

So, I've been playing Hades for awhile now, and man, I could have Sworn I played this game already, or at least a game that I Sworn I played before. Yet somehow, this one shows up like, “Oh you thought you escaped? Cute.” And suddenly I’m 47 runs deep, emotionally attached to a floating head that insults me, and arguing with a god about my work ethic. First off, this game feels illegal in how polished it is. Like, the developers and QA really knew what they were doing. The PM clearly ran flawless retrospectives, and the UAT testers’ feedback actually mattered. Somewhere out there is a Jira board that achieved enlightenment. It seems like this game delivers on multiple levels: Gameplay: Addictive. Not “just one more run,” but “oops it’s 2 AM and I’m negotiating with my alarm clock.” Combat: Fast, smooth, and somehow makes button mashing feel like a deliberate art form. Progression: You die. A lot. But instead of rage-quitting, you’re like, “Ah yes, I have learned nothing. Let’s go again immediately.” Storyline: Surprisingly good. Like, “why am I emotionally invested in Greek family drama?” good. Speaking of story—the character you play (Zagreus, aka “Professional Son Disappointment”) is hilarious and witty. Every time he dies—and he WILL die—he strolls back into the House like he just got back from Costco. Meanwhile, his dad is basically the CEO of Toxic Management™, and their conversations feel like annual performance reviews from hell. Literally. The soundtrack? Eerie and enchanting. It’s the kind of music that makes you feel powerful while simultaneously reminding you that you are, in fact, getting absolutely wrecked by a butterfly with anger issues. The mobs and bosses are all top notch. Each one has personality, style, and a personal vendetta against your hopes and dreams. You’ll go from “I’ve got this!” to “I have made a terrible mistake” in about 3 seconds flat. Now, the storyline does get a bit cringey near the end of a run. There are moments where you’re like, “Wow, this is deep,” immediately followed by, “Okay but did we need that much emotional vulnerability right before I got flattened?” But it does have meaning… eventually… probably… after your 83rd attempt. Also: You can pet the dog. 10/10 Game of the Year. Every character is either incredibly attractive, deeply mysterious, or both. I don’t trust it. The game rewards you for dying, which is great because I am extremely talented at that. Final verdict: Hades is what happens when a game respects your time, your intelligence, and your inevitable failure—all at once. It’s beautiful, brutal, and somehow comforting in a “welcome back, loser” kind of way. Would I recommend it? Absolutely. Will it consume your life? Also absolutely. Will you escape? Absolutely not tied in a knot.

Hades it a top down hack-and-slash game. There are roguelike elements, but the player is mostly challenged with clearing four zones and four bosses. It takes twenty to forty minutes to fully do this, but there are so many different weapons and abilities and ways to modify a run; that a player will not be bored in repeating their efforts to escape Hades. This is a great game. If I had to describe it one word, I'd say it is polished. As a roguelike, it heavily incentivizes you to try things you haven't before, which prevents repetitive gameplay. As an example, I'd gotten a successful run in less than 20 runs, but I ended playing till about 80 runs in order to complete various quests and stories, unlocking all achievements. The animations, music, combat are a treat. A successful run can take anywhere from a little more than 15 mins to an hour. But the story does not end with a successful run. There's a lot of side stories, and the game does not feel like a grind thanks to the myriad of combinations. Can highly recommend the game to anyone playing a hack and slash type, probably a great way to enter the roguelike genre too!

Hades is a incredibly solid roguelite. The gameplay loop is satisfying, the visuals are nice, and the storylines and lore wrap it up into a solid package. While the game is a roguelite, it does by default align closer to roguelike on difficulty. Luckily mods do exist that allow you to tweak the game to whatever works for you. The game is amazing but I do have to ask what more could this game have been. Pros: -Incredibly well done and solid visuals -Incredibly well done combat systems -Well written story -God mode is an amazing addition doubly so that it doesnt invalidate achievements. cons: -The difficulty is unique. while the game provides tool so counter it, almost all the tools stop just before it truly made the game work well for me. The systems felt capped early to make the game take longer to play more so than balancing it. -Towards the later parts where i was achievement hunting, the RNG was quite annoying. some storylines require an NPC to say 3 separate lines of which they can say 1 per run. needless to say add in the npc being a chance of spawning and you end up doing multiple runs hoping to see one more line of dialog. -The game never really gave you tools to adjust the run freely. While the pact of punishment does enable some, there was no way to make zones be longer, limit gods, or other advanced tweaks in the base game.

An Incredible action game with a beautiful story about family and wonderful art style and music, this game uses it's gameplay elements in a very interesting way to tell an engaging story that progresses very smoothly with your pace at the same time that challenges you to keep trying to get better in order to escape hell. The characters are all very unique and interesting, and the way the story references the original myths on which the characters are based on but still brings new interpretations for them are very fun to see. I usually don't play a lot of roguelike/roguelite games for so long, but the way that I was rewarded with story and totally new interactions every time I got back to Hades's house kept me very immersed in the world of this game.

A genuine fun dive into hell itself. Detailed environments and frustrating enemies. Love the gameplay, story alike and would recommend to anyone wanting something special that's quick to pick up and put down. Much to unlock in both lore and combat.

The game has such great mechanics and combat, especially once you find the style of fighting that really fits for you, as it gives you a plethora of options and tools to explore and experiment with. The music and all of the environments you roll through are incredibly beautiful. And. Man. All of the designs. I mentioned the environments already but the character designs, the designs for the weaponry, for the flourishes surrounding attacks and abilities as you fight, for little collectibles and items, even for something like the menu are so detailed and wonderful to look at. I appreciate the way this game tackles and represents Greek Mythology. The gods and goddesses, and even the heroes of old that also are present in the game, all feel fairly portrayed and really seem to fit with how they are in their myths, neither good nor bad but just… beings with flaws and strengths like the rest of us. There’s still some creative liberties taken with how things are portrayed in the Underworld, specifically with the environments and some of the enemies, but it still manages to feel really fun and entertaining regardless. Hades is still an antagonist, a role I feel he's unfairly thrown into in a lot of media, but it feels a lot more fair and understandable with him being a dad to your player character, who is currently going through a rebellious period. Truly this was just a joy of a game and is definitely worth checking out. Roguelikes tend to be hard for people not already a fan of them to get into, but I hear that it's an easier task with this game than other titles, and it does try and make it more accessible to people who might struggle with the gameplay but are interested in experiencing the story.

Artistically handcrafted, narratively engaging, and [b]addictively replayable[/b], Hades expertly demonstrates just how well-made an action roguelite can be through [b]exceptional quality[/b]. Despite the mythological concepts introduced being simplified, these adjustments are better suited here. An energetically action-focused, rewarding gameplay loop ties these aspects together, but the [b]longevity of new content[/b] in challenges, progression, and additional details keeps this experience fresh long into your playthrough. A must-play game for the genre.

Everything has personality and polish. It’s one of those games where you stop for a second just to appreciate how good it looks. The gameplay is just as strong. Combat is fast, responsive, and incredibly satisfying. Every weapon feels different, every run feels slightly unique because of the boons, and experimenting with builds never gets boring. Dying never feels pointless because the progression system and story keep moving forward. And the characters are amazing. The writing, the voice acting, the relationships. You actually care about talking to everyone after each run. The world feels alive, even though you’re technically repeating the same escape attempt over and over. I genuinely have nothing to complain about. The balance, the music, the pacing, the replayability. Everything works together perfectly. For me, this game is as close to perfect as it gets.

Every run gives you something new to look forward to. The combat is smooth and satisfying, especially when you get a good combination of boons. Hades is one of those rare games that grabs you from the first run and somehow keeps getting better every time you die. Supergiant Games has absolutely nailed the roguelike formula — tight, satisfying combat, layered storytelling, and gorgeous presentation all woven together seamlessly. Every escape attempt as Zagreus feels unique thanks to the huge variety of weapons, boons, and upgrades from the Olympian gods. The writing is sharp, full of personality, and makes every character feel alive (and weirdly relatable — even the god of death). What really stands out is how the narrative evolves through repeated failure — the game expects you to die, and uses it to deepen the story and world instead of punishing you. The art direction is stunning, the voice acting is top-tier, and Darren Korb’s soundtrack absolutely rips — it’s easily one of the best game soundtracks out there. Whether you’re a roguelike veteran or new to the genre, Hades is pure, addictive brilliance. There’s always something new to discover, and the gameplay loop is so satisfying it’s almost dangerous. Pros: - Incredibly polished combat - Deep and rewarding progression - Amazing writing and characters - One of the best soundtracks in gaming Cons: - You will lose sleep trying to “just do one more run” Final Verdict: A masterpiece of design and storytelling. Worth every drop of ichor.

Hades is one of the best rogue-likes ever made. The combat is fast, smooth, and incredibly satisfying, with each weapon offering its own playstyle and endless build possibilities thanks to the Olympian boons. Every run teaches you something, and even when you die, it never feels wasted.

Hades is one of the tightest, most addictive action roguelikes ever made. The combat is fast and responsive, the weapons feel meaningfully different, and the power-ups encourage experimentation without overwhelming the player. Every run feels purposeful, and the constant trickle of story and character interaction makes failure feel like progress rather than punishment. If I have any beef with the game, it’s its light smattering of the rainbow flag, though it’s generally mild and unobtrusive. It rarely interferes with the core experience and is easy to overlook compared to how strong the gameplay, art direction, music, and voice acting are overall. Hades succeeds because it puts mechanics and player engagement first, delivering a near-perfect loop that remains fun for dozens of hours. Even with minor nitpicks, it’s an easy recommendation and a modern classic in the genre.

A fast-paced roguelike action game where each run through the underworld offers different abilities, enemies, and build possibilities. The combat is extremely responsive and satisfying, and even for someone not usually strong in action games, it feels learnable and rewarding over time. The narrative is also a major highlight, with constant new dialogue and character interactions that make repeated runs feel meaningful rather than repetitive. Eventually, progression becomes tied to higher difficulty clears, and I hit a skill ceiling I couldn’t fully overcome, but I still got a huge amount of enjoyment and value out of it.

I didn’t expect to get this hooked—but Hades completely pulled me in. Everything just works. The combat is fast, responsive, and insanely satisfying once you start chaining builds together. Every run feels different thanks to the variety of boons, weapons, and upgrades, so it never gets stale even after dozens of attempts. What really surprised me though is the storytelling. For a roguelike, the characters feel alive. The dialogue is sharp, often funny, and somehow they made dying over and over actually feel like part of the journey instead of a punishment. The art style is beautiful, the voice acting is top-tier, and the soundtrack hits hard during intense fights. If you’re into action games, or even if you’re not usually a fan of roguelikes, this is one of those rare games that just clicks. Easy to pick up, hard to put down. 10/10 — “just one more run” turns into 3 hours real quick.

This game teaches how to make gameplay and, most of all, a story evolve throughout a genre focused on repetition: roguelike. Through the always new and coherent dialogues and scenes, you really feel like you're progressively getting closer to your final goal, despite keeping dying and repeating always the same path, same rooms fighting the same enemies, while proceeding and improving at your own pace. The action component also has so much variety to never feel repetitive and still make you want to try new things (at least for my first 15h). However, here, I could argue that combat is quite messy, more of a spam of attacks and dashes, because you can't really see clearly what's happening with all those lights, and also, given the high health of enemies, it's clearly a game about spamming rather than few precise blows. But playing feels very good and responsive.

This is a difficult game to recommend. The combat often feels slow, the enemies are bullet sponges, and worst of all the upgrade system doesn't feel impactful. Every run feels the exact same. Hades succeeds in pulling in even people who don't play rouge-lites due to the way it handles death, even if you die in the first room multiple times it's likely characters will have new dialogue. The game takes the edge of death and makes it less of a punishment and more a narrative tool. So how's gameplay? Well very good to be blunt. In essence this game is similar to diablo, in which it's a top down rpg in which you hack and slash your way through various dungeons all with greek mythology serving as the backdrop. You pick powers from different gods, using a variety of interesting weapons and fight hordes of enemies only to die and do it all again. Combat is incredibly fast and fluid with the build variety being quite staggering. The more you play the more the game hands out new systems which keeps the repetitive nature of the game fresh. Story, music, presentation are all top quality. As mentioned the amount of dialogue is insane but it would mean nothing if the voice acting sucked or if the story was uninteresting. Thankfully this is a game that delivers on all fronts, characters are memorable, the main character zagreus is enduring and the titular Hades is intimidating. I think my only issue is the fact that some areas and bosses do get quite samey and build variety whilst varied does start falling into the meta trap when you just want to start smashing out clears. For pure rouge-lite I'd always lean towards dead cells but for the simple experience of a good game, hades is unmatched. In short Hades is fantastic, that one of a kind game that has bridged the gap for a genre that was quite niche and brought it into the mainstream, hades has been an incredible gane bringing in many to the genre and has gone on to show the narrative power only games can achieve.

Hades is a roguelite action game built around Zagreus, the son of Hades, as he repeatedly attempts to escape the Underworld. On paper, it follows a familiar run-based structure, but what makes it exceptional is how every failed escape feels meaningful. Instead of treating death as a reset, the game turns it into progression, storytelling, character development, and motivation to try again. The combat is fast, responsive, and endlessly satisfying. Each weapon feels distinct, and the Boons from Olympian gods constantly reshape how a run plays out. One attempt might revolve around lightning-fast melee aggression, while another becomes a ranged build focused on poison, deflection, or critical damage. The game encourages experimentation without making failure feel punishing, and its balance is strong enough that almost every build can become viable with the right choices. What truly elevates Hades is how seamlessly it blends gameplay and narrative. Characters remember your attempts, comment on your progress, and evolve over time through conversations, gifts, and side stories. The writing is sharp, funny, emotional, and remarkably consistent. Even after dozens of runs, there is still new dialogue to uncover, which makes the Underworld feel alive rather than repetitive. Progression is excellent. Permanent upgrades, weapon aspects, keepsakes, house renovations, and relationship systems all give you reasons to keep playing beyond simply reaching the surface. The game constantly rewards effort in small but meaningful ways, creating one of the most addictive loops in the genre. Even when a run goes badly, you usually come away with resources, knowledge, or new story moments. The presentation is outstanding. The art style is bold and expressive, the soundtrack is incredible, and the voice acting gives every character personality. From the House of Hades to the chaos of combat, every part of the game feels polished and intentional. It is stylish without sacrificing readability, which is especially important in such a fast-paced game. There are very few real weaknesses. Some late-game progression can become grindy, especially when chasing specific upgrades or story resolutions, and repeated areas naturally lose a little surprise over time. But these are minor issues in a game that remains engaging far longer than most roguelites. [hr][/hr] [b]Highlights:[/b] [list] [*]Fast, precise, and highly satisfying combat [*]Excellent weapon variety and build experimentation [*]Brilliant integration of roguelite structure and storytelling [*]Memorable characters with consistently strong writing [*]Rewarding progression that makes every run feel worthwhile [*]Outstanding art direction, music, and voice acting [*]Late-game progression can become slightly grindy [/list] [hr][/hr] [b]TL;DR:[/b] Hades is a near-perfect roguelite that combines sharp combat, meaningful progression, and exceptional storytelling into one of the most polished games in the genre. Every failed run still feels rewarding, every character adds personality, and every system works together to keep the experience fresh, addictive, and memorable.

The soundtrack is electrifying, the art direction is gorgeous, and the world design drips with atmosphere. What truly elevates Hades, though, is its cast: every character, from Zagreus and the Olympian gods to the denizens of the House of Hades, is beautifully written, voiced, and full of heart. Their intertwined stories give weight to every death and make each escape attempt feel meaningful. Hades is a roguelite action game built around Zagreus, the son of Hades, as he repeatedly attempts to escape the Underworld. On paper, it follows a familiar run-based structure, but what makes it exceptional is how every failed escape feels meaningful. Instead of treating death as a reset, the game turns it into progression, storytelling, character development, and motivation to try again. The combat is fast, responsive, and endlessly satisfying. Each weapon feels distinct, and the Boons from Olympian gods constantly reshape how a run plays out. One attempt might revolve around lightning-fast melee aggression, while another becomes a ranged build focused on poison, deflection, or critical damage. The game encourages experimentation without making failure feel punishing, and its balance is strong enough that almost every build can become viable with the right choices. What truly elevates Hades is how seamlessly it blends gameplay and narrative. Characters remember your attempts, comment on your progress, and evolve over time through conversations, gifts, and side stories. The writing is sharp, funny, emotional, and remarkably consistent. Even after dozens of runs, there is still new dialogue to uncover, which makes the Underworld feel alive rather than repetitive. Progression is excellent. Permanent upgrades, weapon aspects, keepsakes, house renovations, and relationship systems all give you reasons to keep playing beyond simply reaching the surface. The game constantly rewards effort in small but meaningful ways, creating one of the most addictive loops in the genre. Even when a run goes badly, you usually come away with resources, knowledge, or new story moments. The presentation is outstanding. The art style is bold and expressive, the soundtrack is incredible, and the voice acting gives every character personality. From the House of Hades to the chaos of combat, every part of the game feels polished and intentional. It is stylish without sacrificing readability, which is especially important in such a fast-paced game. There are very few real weaknesses. Some late-game progression can become grindy, especially when chasing specific upgrades or story resolutions, and repeated areas naturally lose a little surprise over time. But these are minor issues in a game that remains engaging far longer than most roguelites. [hr][/hr] [b]Highlights:[/b] [list] [*]Fast, precise, and highly satisfying combat [*]Excellent weapon variety and build experimentation [*]Brilliant integration of roguelite structure and storytelling [*]Memorable characters with consistently strong writing [*]Rewarding progression that makes every run feel worthwhile [*]Outstanding art direction, music, and voice acting [*]Late-game progression can become slightly grindy [/list] [hr][/hr] [b]TL;DR:[/b] Hades is a near-perfect roguelite that combines sharp combat, meaningful progression, and exceptional storytelling into one of the most polished games in the genre. Every failed run still feels rewarding, every character adds personality, and every system works together to keep the experience fresh, addictive, and memorable.

review_text: I have never been naturally drawn to pixel art games. The visual style usually makes it harder for me to feel invested. However, I have always loved farming games, and Harvest Moon Back to Nature shaped a significant part of my childhood. I spent a large amount of my primary school years playing it. It brings together everything I wished HM BTN could have expanded on, while still respecting the charm and simplicity of classic farming titles. The inclusion of multiplayer is a major advantage. It allows for cooperative play and makes the game more accessible for me to share with my child. This flexibility adds depth without compromising the core experience. The ongoing support from the developer is also remarkable. Continuous updates, thoughtful improvements, and the clear passion behind the project elevate the game far beyond standard expectations. I genuinely appreciate the developer, his partner, and every individual involved in making this game what it is. At this point, I have found very little to criticise. A less blocky visual option would be a welcome addition, but it is not essential. The pixel art style has its own identity and contributes to the atmosphere in a meaningful way. Overall, Stardew Valley succeeds not only as a farming game, but as a deeply crafted, well-balanced experience that rewards time, curiosity, and care.

You play as a tired corpo slave who ditches the corpo life for chill farm life, eventually choosing between saving the local community or letting a big corporation take over. Many say to not do a modded playthrough the first time but I would say honestly give it a shot if the game doesn't interest you in some aspects. Titanfall 2 is one of the most underrated shooters of the last decade, delivering an exceptional blend of fast-paced action and a surprisingly emotional single-player campaign. Missions constantly introduce new mechanics such as time-shifting between past and present or gravity-defying platforming that keep gameplay fresh and inventive. The relationship between Cooper and BT adds genuine heart, making the story far more memorable than most FPS campaigns. Gameplay is where Titanfall 2 truly shines. The movement system—wall-running, sliding, double-jumping feels incredibly fluid and rewarding, encouraging speed and creativity rather than slow, cover-based combat. Pilots and Titans are both satisfying to control, and switching between agile infantry combat and the raw power of Titans creates an exciting rhythm that few shooters can match. Visually, the game still holds up well, with detailed environments, strong art direction, and smooth performance. I don’t usually write long reviews for games, but Titanfall 2 honestly deserves it. It’s one of those rare games that surprised me in the best possible way. I picked it up expecting a fun shooter, but what I got was a game with an amazing campaign, incredibly smooth gameplay, and one of the most enjoyable multiplayer experiences I’ve had in years. The single-player story is much better than I expected from a shooter like this. You play as Jack Cooper, a rifleman who ends up bonding with a Titan named BT-7274 after his commander dies in battle. What starts as a simple military mission slowly turns into a really emotional journey between a pilot and his Titan. BT isn’t just a machine that you call into battle - he actually feels like a real companion. Throughout the campaign you build a connection with him through dialogue, teamwork, and the situations you go through together. Some moments in the story are surprisingly touching, and by the end of the campaign I was way more invested than I expected. The missions themselves are incredibly creative. Instead of repeating the same shooting gallery over and over again, the game constantly introduces new mechanics. One level has you switching between two timelines in the middle of combat, another takes place in a factory that literally assembles entire buildings while you fight through it. It keeps the campaign feeling fresh the whole time, and I never felt bored or like I was just doing the same thing again and again. The gameplay is where Titanfall 2 really shines. The movement system is fantastic. Running on walls, sliding across the ground, jumping between rooftops, and chaining all those moves together feels incredibly smooth and natural. Once you get the hang of it, you feel almost unstoppable flying across the map. It’s one of those games where simply moving around is fun by itself. And then there are the Titans. Calling down a giant mech in the middle of a battle never gets old. Each Titan has its own abilities and weapons, which makes them feel very different from each other. Some are built for heavy damage, others are more tactical, and learning how to use them properly adds another layer of strategy to the game. The multiplayer is just as impressive. It’s fast, chaotic, and incredibly satisfying once you learn the movement system. Unlike many shooters where players move slowly and fights happen around corners, Titanfall 2 encourages constant motion. Players are running across walls, jumping across buildings, and dropping Titans onto the battlefield. It creates these huge, cinematic battles that feel unlike anything else. What I also like about the multiplayer is that it stays accessible. Even if you’re not the best player in the lobby, you can still contribute by fighting AI enemies, helping your team earn points, and working toward calling down your Titan. That makes the matches feel exciting even when you’re still learning the game. Visually, the game still looks great even years after release. The environments are detailed, the Titan designs are fantastic, and the animations are incredibly smooth. The sound design is also excellent - the heavy footsteps of Titans, the roar of weapons, and the music during intense battles all add a lot to the atmosphere. Overall, Titanfall 2 is easily one of the most underrated shooters ever made. The campaign is creative and emotional, the gameplay is incredibly smooth, and the multiplayer is both intense and fun. It’s the kind of game that reminds you why shooters can still be exciting when developers try something different. If you enjoy fast-paced action, great movement mechanics, and a surprisingly strong story, Titanfall 2 is absolutely worth playing. It’s a game that I still come back to, and every time I do, it reminds me just how special it is.

The movement is incredible, wall-running, sliding, double-jumping - it’s pure momentum-driven joy. Combat on foot feels sharp and skillful. Calling down your Titan feels powerful every single time. Vince Zampella didn’t chase trends. He set standards. A timeless shooter, still ahead of its time.

Titanfall 2 is a fast, stylish shooter about parkour, giant robots, and does something rare: it tells a complete, memorable story in a tight package. There’s no bloated open world. No checklist obsession. No cinematic excess. Just clever level design, strong pacing, and one time-manipulation level that casually reminds the industry what creativity looks like. And then it emotionally blindsides you with a war machine who understands sacrifice better than the humans around him . BT is a Titan. He is programmed for combat, tactics, and survival. He speaks in calm, precise statements. He does not joke. He does not hesitate. And yet somehow, he is the most emotionally intelligent character in the entire game. BT listens. BT trusts you. He doesn’t say “I care.” He says, “Protocol 3: Protect the Pilot.” And somehow that hits harder. The art style does the heavy lifting. Strong silhouettes, bold colors, and readable environments make the game look sharp without needing ultra-realistic textures. The movement is incredible, wall-running, sliding, double-jumping - it’s pure momentum-driven joy. Combat on foot feels sharp and skillful. Calling down your Titan feels powerful every single time. Vince Zampella didn’t chase trends. He set standards. A timeless shooter, still ahead of its time.

Titanfall 2 is an outstanding FPS with one of the best single-player stories in the genre. Combining a strong narrative with fast, fluid shooting is a genius idea, and it’s executed beautifully. Verdict: One of the most mechanically refined shooters ever made, with a campaign that still sets the bar for FPS design. Titanfall 2’s greatest strength is how fluidly it blends movement, gunplay, and verticality. Wall-running, sliding, and grappling are not gimmicks—they are fundamental to how combat flows. The result is a shooter where positioning and momentum matter as much as aim. The single-player campaign deserves special mention. Each level introduces a new mechanic and fully explores it before moving on, avoiding repetition while constantly teaching the player something new. The relationship between pilot and Titan is handled with surprising emotional weight, elevating the narrative beyond typical FPS storytelling. Multiplayer remains fast, skill-based, and rewarding, though the player base can feel uneven at times due to matchmaking population swings. Still, when matches click, few shooters offer the same sense of kinetic satisfaction. What Works Well Exceptional movement mechanics One of the best FPS campaigns ever made Clear visual and mechanical readability High skill ceiling without feeling unfair What Needs Improvement Multiplayer population inconsistency Limited long-term content support Final Thoughts: Titanfall 2 is a masterclass in FPS design. It may not have the ongoing support of newer titles, but its core gameplay remains unmatched.

review_text: I can't speak to the multiplayer of this game, but as for the single player- I have a handful of criticisms. the final boss is too easy and a bit anticlimactic, the overarching story is cliche at best, and none of the characters stand out much aside from perhaps the interactions between the main character cooper and his titan BT. it's also a bit on the short side clocking in at 4 hours for one playthrough on standard difficulty. in light of how dead the multiplayer is I can't say you should buy it full price. with those out of the way everything else about this game is practically perfect. simply moving feels wonderful. the gunplay feels wonderful. the gameplay variety and pacing are interlinked in a way that makes the mere act of progressing the story feel fluid. everything in the game seems to be in the service of momentum. every new tool, each level specific gimmick, the basic moveset of the character itself, all of it is there to help you keep moving around and hardly ever stop if you so wish. each setpiece is wonderfully created and awe inspiring. they are a scifi game and wear that on their sleeve, showing you sights and sounds that can probably never be recreated in reality. more than once I had audibly said "woah" or "that's cool"- and most games don't get that kind of response from me. it is the epitome of everything a linear military shooter can be. if the campaign was twice as long I'd say buy it even at full price but as is the length of it means you gotta wait for a better price ratio. but do play it someday if you've got any interest whatsoever in this kind of game. you will not be disappointed.

Hades is one of those rare games that grabs you from the first run and somehow keeps getting better every time you die. Supergiant Games has absolutely nailed the roguelike formula — tight, satisfying combat, layered storytelling, and gorgeous presentation all woven together seamlessly. Every escape attempt as Zagreus feels unique thanks to the huge variety of weapons, boons, and upgrades from the Olympian gods. The writing is sharp, full of personality, and makes every character feel alive (and weirdly relatable — even the god of death). What really stands out is how the narrative evolves through repeated failure — the game expects you to die, and uses it to deepen the story and world instead of punishing you. The art direction is stunning, the voice acting is top-tier, and Darren Korb’s soundtrack absolutely rips — it’s easily one of the best game soundtracks out there. Whether you’re a roguelike veteran or new to the genre, Hades is pure, addictive brilliance. There’s always something new to discover, and the gameplay loop is so satisfying it’s almost dangerous. Pros: - Incredibly polished combat - Deep and rewarding progression - Amazing writing and characters - One of the best soundtracks in gaming Cons: - You will lose sleep trying to “just do one more run” Final Verdict: A masterpiece of design and storytelling. Worth every drop of ichor.

Of course I enjoyed CP2077, but I almost want to give it a negative rating to emphasize why I think it's merely a "really good" game as opposed to an "incredible" one. The storyline was a highlight (compelling and with choices that mattered), but there is very little mechanically in the game that hasn't been done before: GTA4/5 defined the standard for open worlds decades ago, and any mainline RPG has similar depth for character choices, skill trees, progression etc. So, does CP2077 differentiate with an immersive world that is truly novel? For me, not really. The map is expansive with some incredible artwork, but can feel samey within any given district. The characters, while memorable, are ultimately formulaic. The voice acting was surprisingly lacking in places (male V sounds like he's reading out instructions for a dishwasher). Towards the latter stages of the game, the combat starts to feel mundane due to a lack of enemy diversity. Despite playing with the latest patch (April 2026), the game is still super buggy: floating world items, stuttering animations, glitching quests, CTDs (all of which are perhaps to be expected for a game of this scale, but still no less annoying). I enjoyed my play-through, but don't see a reason to replay any time soon!
