A recent return to Elden Ring finally helped me understand what so many players have been praising for years. After multiple past attempts where the magic just didn’t click, this latest playthrough opened my eyes to how remarkable the game truly is. The world is stunning, with sweeping vistas, intricate ruins, and atmospheric lighting that make every region feel alive. The sound design elevates that sense of place even further—haunting ambient tracks, thunderous boss themes, and crisp combat audio all work together to pull you deeper into the Lands Between. The combat is where everything really came together for me. It’s challenging, sometimes brutally so, but it’s also deliberate, responsive, and endlessly rewarding once the rhythm sets in. What made the difficulty feel more manageable this time was embracing both player summons and spirit ashes. They don’t trivialize the game, but they smooth out the rough edges enough to let the brilliance of the encounters shine through instead of feeling like a wall. After finally “getting it,” I can confidently say Elden Ring is an exceptional experience—one that rewards persistence with moments of awe, triumph, and discovery. 9.5/10.

From the outset, with a story that felt dull and barely existent along with an indie-feel to most other elements: interface, visuals and combat, I could not find a reason to continue, and so I requested—and received—a refund. Thank you.

Where do I begin? By the time I was done with it, the game left me completely disappointed. Most of the negative reviews have captured all the significant problems with this game so I'll keep it (relatively) short. My favorite games in the Fromsoft catalogue are Dark Souls and Sekiro (also among my favorite games of all time). These games feel deliberately designed; Dark Souls made you feel like exploring a dangerous land, and Sekiro's combat system is truly one of a kind. But Elden Ring? It's a video game ass video game. Everything in this game exists for the player's benefit. Side dungeons almost always end in boss fights with a treasure chest to reward the player. Stakes of Marika make it convenient to fight bosses. Sites of Grace abound so that you never feel the tension of exploration (also free fast travel). Every single death in this game will only be due to bosses, or sometimes gravity. Don't wanna fight overworld enemies? Get on Torrent and ride away. The open world is simply a collection of all the dungeons they made spread horizontally. Is the open world truly open then? Nope, there's a strictly linear progression with some side stuff along the way, with arbitrary progression gates like Morgott's Seal and Great rune requirements. Balance is literally non-existent. Is the combat good then? It's basically Dark Souls combat again. There's a gazillion weapons, but they all mostly play the same, you know how it is. Boss fights are now true shonen anime style affairs, wait for your turn and dodge while the boss does his wombo combo and then poke. Repeat all over again for a 100 bosses, and the nail in the coffin is that a significant portion of them are repeats. Not even remembrance bosses are spared. Don't even get me started on the DLC. I was genuinely excited to play this game, and sadly, this made me question the future of Soulslikes from Fromsoft. I guess we'll have to wait and see.

Hades is one of the tightest, most addictive action roguelikes ever made. The combat is fast and responsive, the weapons feel meaningfully different, and the power-ups encourage experimentation without overwhelming the player. Every run feels purposeful, and the constant trickle of story and character interaction makes failure feel like progress rather than punishment. If I have any beef with the game, it’s its light smattering of the rainbow flag, though it’s generally mild and unobtrusive. It rarely interferes with the core experience and is easy to overlook compared to how strong the gameplay, art direction, music, and voice acting are overall. Hades succeeds because it puts mechanics and player engagement first, delivering a near-perfect loop that remains fun for dozens of hours. Even with minor nitpicks, it’s an easy recommendation and a modern classic in the genre.

A fast-paced roguelike action game where each run through the underworld offers different abilities, enemies, and build possibilities. The combat is extremely responsive and satisfying, and even for someone not usually strong in action games, it feels learnable and rewarding over time. Run variety is one of its strongest aspects—no two runs feel the same, and experimenting with different builds stays fun throughout. The narrative is also a major highlight, with constant new dialogue and character interactions that make repeated runs feel meaningful rather than repetitive. Eventually, progression becomes tied to higher difficulty clears, and I hit a skill ceiling I couldn’t fully overcome, but I still got a huge amount of enjoyment and value out of it.

Hades is one of those rare games that feels razor‑sharp from the first run and only gets better the deeper you go. Supergiant Games blends fast, responsive combat with a roguelike structure that never feels punishing for the sake of it. Every attempt to escape the Underworld pushes you forward narratively as well as mechanically, which is a big part of why the loop is so addictive. The writing is surprisingly warm and witty, giving each Olympian and Underworld resident a distinct personality. Even after dozens of runs, new dialogue keeps appearing, making the world feel alive rather than repetitive. On PC, the game runs beautifully — smooth performance, crisp art direction, and a soundtrack that hits with real energy.

Safe to say - a modern day classic, with how well-written the plot and the conversations are with how thought-out and satisfying the combat, its roguelike nature, the dating sim and every other character interaction are. Humor radiates through every dialogue line, meanwhile being well balanced-out by dramatic main and sub-quests. The soundtrack ♥♥♥♥♥, the voice acting is entirely cinematic, the ending and the epilogue don't quite feel like goodbye, so staying for a couple more runs to complete the remaining achievements doesn't feel bad. Lots of games about the Living could only wish to be able to breathe nearly as much life force into the audience as this game about the Dead does.

I didn’t expect to get this hooked—but Hades completely pulled me in. Everything just works. The combat is fast, responsive, and insanely satisfying once you start chaining builds together. Every run feels different thanks to the variety of boons, weapons, and upgrades, so it never gets stale even after dozens of attempts. What really surprised me though is the storytelling. For a roguelike, the characters feel alive. The dialogue is sharp, often funny, and somehow they made dying over and over actually feel like part of the journey instead of a punishment. The art style is beautiful, the voice acting is top-tier, and the soundtrack hits hard during intense fights. If you’re into action games, or even if you’re not usually a fan of roguelikes, this is one of those rare games that just clicks. Easy to pick up, hard to put down. 10/10 — “just one more run” turns into 3 hours real quick.

This game teaches how to make gameplay and, most of all, a story evolve throughout a genre focused on repetition: roguelike. Through the always new and coherent dialogues and scenes, you really feel like you're progressively getting closer to your final goal, despite keeping dying and repeating always the same path, same rooms fighting the same enemies, while proceeding and improving at your own pace. The action component also has so much variety to never feel repetitive and still make you want to try new things (at least for my first 15h). However, here, I could argue that combat is quite messy, more of a spam of attacks and dashes, because you can't really see clearly what's happening with all those lights, and also, given the high health of enemies, it's clearly a game about spamming rather than few precise blows. But playing feels very good and responsive.
Fun roguelite with engaging story. 100% does start to feel grindy towards the end, but overall a good game. 8/10

You play as a tired corpo slave who ditches the corpo life for chill farm life, eventually choosing between saving the local community or letting a big corporation take over. The NPCs aren't just cardboard cutouts either. They’ve got real depth and deal with heavy, relatable stuff, which makes befriending or romancing them feel way more meaningful. Plus, the whole thing looks like a gorgeous 16-bit dream and has a soundtrack that’s absolute fire.

Titanfall 2 is a fast, stylish shooter about parkour, giant robots, and does something rare: it tells a complete, memorable story in a tight package. There’s no bloated open world. No checklist obsession. No cinematic excess. Just clever level design, strong pacing, and one time-manipulation level that casually reminds the industry what creativity looks like. And then it emotionally blindsides you with a war machine who understands sacrifice better than the humans around him . BT is a Titan. He is programmed for combat, tactics, and survival. He speaks in calm, precise statements. He does not joke. He does not hesitate. And yet somehow, he is the most emotionally intelligent character in the entire game. BT listens. BT trusts you. He doesn’t say “I care.” He says, “Protocol 3: Protect the Pilot.” And somehow that hits harder. The art style does the heavy lifting. Strong silhouettes, bold colors, and readable environments make the game look sharp without needing ultra-realistic textures. The movement is incredible, wall-running, sliding, double-jumping - it’s pure momentum-driven joy. Combat on foot feels sharp and skillful. Calling down your Titan feels powerful every single time. Vince Zampella didn’t chase trends. He set standards. A timeless shooter, still ahead of its time.

[h3]APEX[/h3] ★★★☆ 7, awesome Titanfall 2’s campaign is one of the most polished among the multiplayer-focused titles, perfectly blending platformer, pilot combat, and Titan combat without a single dull moment. Titanfall 2’s pilot has no fall damage and can wall-run, slide, and double-jump, allowing them to perform high-speed acrobatics in platformer and combat. The Arc Tool puzzle and platformer utilizing time machine are intuitive without being too predictable, giving life to the middle of the campaign where similar landscapes tend to repeat. Pilot combat allows you to fight while using movement skills, so flying through the air to ambush enemies is rather good, but utilizing that speed in a tussle—like the pipe facility battle—is more thrilling. And what about Titan combat? Switching between various weapon loadouts, the weighty impact of combat is visceral. Especially in the mission of “Titanfall,” when you wield the Ronin and slice through Titans, the thrill becomes almost euphoric. Its boss battles could be the only downside. Rather than featuring unique mechanics, they essentially consist of versions of previously encountered Titans with merely higher health. It's difficult to dismount from BT and fight as a pilot, and since they differ little from common Titan combat, they fail to fully realize Titanfall 2’s potential.

If I could give this game a "mixed" I absolutely would. This game is utterly fantastic. It has incredible environments and exploration, so good that that aspect alone carried me through 3 playthroughs. The boss fights, when done well, are extremely rewarding and feel like a hard yet fair challenge. It's everything else that drags it down for me. The terrible boss fights are *really* terrible. So much so that they drag down the experience for a while. Also, the quest design in this game is bafflingly bad. They tried to keep the vague, cryptic quests of the original Souls games and put them in an open world format where 90% of players will likely never return to the specific area the NPC decided to move to. Of course there are hints to where they've gone, but unless you've got a notebook keeping track of it there's no way to follow all 10-20 questlines organically. That said I don't think the quests even add much to the game and you can beat the game without progressing any of them. There's a lot to love about this game, and even more to learn to love. Yet the downsides can't be ignored. This game is a trailblazer yet suffers from some obvious flaws that just kinda carried over from past games. I guess whether or not you should buy this game is how much you're able to tolerate and if the highs of this game resonate with you, which it definitely did for me.

It’s not just about action—there’s depth, moral ambiguity, and plenty of moments that stick with you even after you log off. Gameplay-wise, the flexibility is impressive. Whether you prefer stealth, hacking, or going in guns blazing, the game gives you the freedom to shape your own playstyle. The skill system and upgrades allow for a lot of experimentation, which keeps things fresh over time. Visually, the game looks stunning, especially on a well-optimized setup. Cyberpunk 2077 delivers a rich open-world experience, strong storytelling, and enjoyable gameplay mechanics. It’s a game that’s easy to get lost in, and one I’d definitely recommend to anyone looking for a deep and visually impressive RPG.

Overview After 134 hours with Forza Horizon 5, it is clear this is a game that knows how to keep you hooked. It is smooth, polished, and easy to enjoy, but the longer you play, the more certain cracks start to show beneath the surface. Pros Visually Impressive World Mexico looks stunning. The environments are varied, from deserts and jungles to coastlines, and everything is detailed and well crafted. From a visual standpoint, it is hard to complain. Driving Feels Just Right The handling is where the game really shines. It is accessible without being boring, and whether you are racing seriously or just cruising, it feels consistently good. Massive Car Collection There is a huge range of vehicles to choose from. You are never really short on options, and experimenting with different builds keeps things interesting. Freedom in Gameplay You are not forced into anything. You can race, explore, tune, or just drive around. That flexibility makes it easy to pick up anytime. Long Lasting Appeal Even after 134 hours, it still has moments that pull you back in. The core gameplay loop is strong enough to hold attention over time. Cons World Feels Empty Over Time While the map looks beautiful, it can start to feel lifeless. Outside of events, there is not much happening dynamically, which makes long drives feel a bit hollow after a while. Repetitive Event Structure Many races and challenges start blending into each other. You notice the repetition more the longer you play. Weak Story Presence The story is minimal and forgettable. It does not add much to the overall experience. Online Inconsistencies Multiplayer is not always reliable. Connection issues and matchmaking problems can take away from the experience. AI Balance Issues The AI can feel uneven, either too easy or oddly difficult at times. Underwhelming Engine Sounds A noticeable drawback. Many cars lack distinct, powerful sound profiles, which takes away from the immersion, especially for a car focused game. Final Verdict Forza Horizon 5 gets the fundamentals right, driving, visuals, and accessibility, but it does not always maintain depth in the long run. It is a great game to jump into, but over time, the emptiness of the world and repetition start to stand out. Still, if you enjoy open world racing, it is worth experiencing.

review_text: 5/5 stars Elden Ring is special. I feel like FromSoft has been building up to this game since the first release of Dark Souls, possibly longer. This game is extremely well made and stunning in every sense of the word. I can talk about how beautiful the world is, how amazing the story is, how fine tuned and gratifying the combat is, how much fun it is to explore but I know you have heard that all before. As someone who has played DS1, DS3 and Bloodborne I am used to some of the basic knowledge of how these games work. It is tricky though, because this game falls victim to one of the sharpest learning curves out there. It is difficult to call this a negative because I feel that this is part of what makes this game so special. I am a firm believer that this game would not work in a world without the internet. I feel like the meta of searching how to do some niche thing and finding an entire community of passionate people enjoying the game is part of the experience itself. Talking with your friends who have played it and explaining different tactics, gear, secrets and more is part of the fun. This game is not friendly, and I am not referring to the fact that it is "hard", but that it intentionally does not guide the player in any way. Yes there is a tutorial but most of the games mechanics are not explained in any way and just left for the players to experiment and find themselves. I spent my first 30 hours in the game when it first came out not understanding how Ashes of War worked. Not until I picked the game up again and started over recently did I start to understand how the combat worked fully. I think the best example of this is the story of Elden Ring itself. A player can play hundreds of hours of the game and not understand a single thing of what's going on. Not understanding what NPCs are talking about, not understanding the overarching plot, maybe they dont even understand who Michela is (the key character in the story). Not until I started watching lore videos did I start piecing everything together and start to appreciate the impact someone like George RR Martin had on the creation of this game. Everything is not there to serve you, it just is. I think this is kind of magical in a way, breathing a sense of life into the world, as if it has always been there and you are just a passerby of this breathing beautiful world. This is how all of the mechanics in the game feel, from the exploration to the combat to the obtuse side quests. Its tricky because if it was executed in any other way I would say this is just bad design but I believe it is the intentional fun of it. They want you to research, they want you to learn. By the time you finish Elden Ring for the first time, if you start all over from a new save you will undoubtedly be a better player because you have taken the time to learn and understand how the game works, not just because your end game character is level 150+. This game is not for the causal player, and I am not saying that to gatekeep, I am saying that because I don't think you will be able to enjoy Elden Ring in any casual way, you absolutely have to “lock in”. It's funny to see when people are in the middle of their first playthrough because I have seen it basically take over their consciousness, once it starts, it works its way into your brain and it's hard to not stop thinking about it. I know that happened to me. If you are willing to give Elden Ring your time and energy, you will not regret it. It is absolutely fantastic.

It works well when it does, but enemy design quite often draws it back. On the bright side, there's a hand cannon. And crossbows are finally functional. Open-world nature of this game clashes violently with its DS1-style quest structure - so if you meet a character you think has a quest, read online where to meet them next. But then there's lore, and aesthetic, and all the actually good areas (though those start rather late).

Titanfall 2 is a fast, stylish shooter about parkour, giant robots, and does something rare: it tells a complete, memorable story in a tight package. There’s no bloated open world. No checklist obsession. No cinematic excess. Just clever level design, strong pacing, and one time-manipulation level that casually reminds the industry what creativity looks like. And then it emotionally blindsides you with a war machine who understands sacrifice better than the humans around him . BT is a Titan. He is programmed for combat, tactics, and survival. He speaks in calm, precise statements. He does not joke. He does not hesitate. And yet somehow, he is the most emotionally intelligent character in the entire game. BT listens. BT trusts you. He doesn’t say “I care.” He says, “Protocol 3: Protect the Pilot.” And somehow that hits harder. The art style does the heavy lifting. Strong silhouettes, bold colors, and readable environments make the game look sharp without needing ultra-realistic textures. The movement is incredible, wall-running, sliding, double-jumping - it’s pure momentum-driven joy. Combat on foot feels sharp and skillful. Calling down your Titan feels powerful every single time. Vince Zampella didn’t chase trends. He set standards. A timeless shooter, still ahead of its time.

There are two elements that can undermine replayability, one of them is farming items and the other is long runs. These two can undermine the feeling of replaying a bit, especially farming items, because if you research well enough in long runs, you will see that there is always a shortcut to your destination, but farming items is always torture no matter what you do. The experience of Elden Ring is impressive in scale but underwhelming in variety. The open world looks magnificent, yet exploration often yields repetitive encounters and predictable rewards. Lore is delivered cryptically, requiring significant interpretation, which can enrich immersion but also reduce emotional engagement. Smaller design issues clunky menus and sparse system explanations add friction. I liked aspects of it, particularly the art direction and moments of discovery, but the overall experience feels mechanically stagnant. Towards the end, when you get to the snowy area you're somewhat grateful the later zones are a little smaller and less content-dense. Combat, once you get used to the rules, is a fun dance of swing and dodge timings, and never gets stale. So, I've been playing Hades for awhile now, and man, I could have Sworn I played this game already, or at least a game that I Sworn I played before. Yet somehow, this one shows up like, “Oh you thought you escaped? Cute.” And suddenly I’m 47 runs deep, emotionally attached to a floating head that insults me, and arguing with a god about my work ethic. First off, this game feels illegal in how polished it is. Like, the developers and QA really knew what they were doing. The PM clearly ran flawless retrospectives, and the UAT testers’ feedback actually mattered. Somewhere out there is a Jira board that achieved enlightenment. It seems like this game delivers on multiple levels: Gameplay: Addictive. Not “just one more run,” but “oops it’s 2 AM and I’m negotiating with my alarm clock.” Combat: Fast, smooth, and somehow makes button mashing feel like a deliberate art form. Progression: You die. A lot. But instead of rage-quitting, you’re like, “Ah yes, I have learned nothing. Let’s go again immediately.” Storyline: Surprisingly good. Like, “why am I emotionally invested in Greek family drama?” good. Speaking of story—the character you play (Zagreus, aka “Professional Son Disappointment”) is hilarious and witty. Every time he dies—and he WILL die—he strolls back into the House like he just got back from Costco. Meanwhile, his dad is basically the CEO of Toxic Management™, and their conversations feel like annual performance reviews from hell. Literally. The soundtrack? Eerie and enchanting. It’s the kind of music that makes you feel powerful while simultaneously reminding you that you are, in fact, getting absolutely wrecked by a butterfly with anger issues. The mobs and bosses are all top notch. Each one has personality, style, and a personal vendetta against your hopes and dreams. You’ll go from “I’ve got this!” to “I have made a terrible mistake” in about 3 seconds flat. Now, the storyline does get a bit cringey near the end of a run. There are moments where you’re like, “Wow, this is deep,” immediately followed by, “Okay but did we need that much emotional vulnerability right before I got flattened?” But it does have meaning… eventually… probably… after your 83rd attempt. Also: You can pet the dog. 10/10 Game of the Year. Every character is either incredibly attractive, deeply mysterious, or both. I don’t trust it. The game rewards you for dying, which is great because I am extremely talented at that. Final verdict: Hades is what happens when a game respects your time, your intelligence, and your inevitable failure—all at once. It’s beautiful, brutal, and somehow comforting in a “welcome back, loser” kind of way. Would I recommend it? Absolutely. Will it consume your life? Also absolutely. Will you escape? Absolutely not tied in a knot.

Cyberpunk 2077 has become one of the best modern open world games out there. Night City feels alive with its incredible atmosphere, detailed environments, and immersive cyberpunk aesthetic. The game also delivers a rich and vibrant story filled with memorable characters, deep lore, and a surprising amount of history behind the world and its corporations, gangs, and conflicts. After all the updates and Phantom Liberty expansion, the experience is now much smoother and far more polished than it was at launch. If you enjoy story driven RPGs, futuristic settings, and exploring a world packed with detail, Cyberpunk 2077 is absolutely worth playing. It even runs perfectly on the Steam Deck, which makes exploring Night City on the go even better.

The Redemption of Night City (With Cavéats) I’ve been here since the beginning, and while Cyberpunk 2077 will be studied as a remarkable turnaround, we shouldn't forget that it launched two years too early. CD Projekt Red arguably got a "free pass" for a state they knew wasn't ready, but the current version of the game is finally something remarkable. The Good The World: Night City is visually outstanding. It is easily one of the most detailed environments ever put in a game, and it’s easy to get lost in the atmosphere. Build Variety: Spec-ing your character is a total joy. The game truly allows you to play how you want, making it incredibly approachable regardless of your preferred playstyle. Masterful Side Quests: Some of the darker, gloomier side stories are the best parts of the game. They are masterfully written and stand as great stories in their own right. Combat: Whether you're hacking or shooting, the combat loop is genuinely fun. The Bad The Writing: While the characters are mostly great, the dialogue can often be "cringe." V feels somewhat bland as a protagonist, and the character creation system still feels like it lacks meaningful impact. Navigation: As beautiful as the map is, it just isn’t fun to navigate. Its scale is impressive, but getting from point A to point B often feels like a chore. The "Arasaka" Irony: There is a lot of deserved love for the game now, but let's not forget the corporate decisions behind the launch. In the end, CDPR acted a lot like the megacorps they satirize. Verdict It’s not a solid 5/5, but the story and the sheer detail of the world keep me coming back. It is a must-play for the atmosphere alone, even if the "soul" of the protagonist and the dialogue occasionally miss the mark

9.5/10 TL;DR: A beautifully crafted open world with exceptional combat variety and style along with environments that are bound to leave you startstruck. However, obscure NPC questlines and lack of in-game tracking can make for a frustrating time without external tools if you are looking to explore all. Detailed Review: Pros: - Boss fights feel like an intricate dance, with clear punish windows while still subverting expectations on subsequent attempts with their delayed or unpredictable attacks. - Excellent build diversity, especially hybrid/quality builds like Faith-Arcane or Strength-Intelligence. - Stunning, vast landscapes that encourage exploration due to the mystique they carry. - Dungeons are generally well-designed, with occasional unique gimmicks that break monotony and keep it fresh. Cons: - NPC questlines are rather obscure and difficult to follow organically. - No in-game checklist or tracking for collected items, making completionist runs unnecessarily reliant on external tools like MapGenie (Scadutree Fragments I'm looking at you). - Just like any other FromSoftware game, ELDEN RING also doesn't explain much about its mechanics making it difficult to recommend to a lot of casual players. Shadow of the Erdtree DLC: A very vertical and puzzle like map layout makes it very interesting but also frustrating to navigate the Land of Shadows. The performance is overall worse compared to the base game and a lot of bosses like to do attacks which are too long (almost like cutscenes). Despite all of that, the beautiful landscapes, more weapon variety and a good story made it quite engaging for me.

After spending around 177 hours in Forza Horizon 5, I can confidently say that it is one of the most engaging open-world racing games I have played. The map set in Mexico is vibrant, diverse, and full of life, offering deserts, jungles, beaches, and mountains that make every drive feel fresh. The graphics are impressive, with detailed environments and cars that look almost real, especially when weather effects or lighting change the atmosphere. The gameplay is accessible but still rewarding. Whether you enjoy drifting, racing on asphalt, going off-road, or simply exploring the world, the game gives you complete freedom. The large collection of cars and the tuning system add depth, letting players experiment with different builds and driving styles. This makes the experience fun even after many hours of play. However, the game also has a few weaknesses. After long sessions, some activities start to feel repetitive, and certain story missions lack impact. The formula does not innovate much compared to previous titles, so experienced players may notice familiar patterns. Even so, Forza Horizon 5 remains an excellent racing game. Its beautiful world, huge variety of cars, and relaxed but exciting gameplay make it worth playing for many hours. For me, it has been a memorable experience, and it still has plenty to offer even after 177 hours on the road.

Overview After 134 hours with Forza Horizon 5, it is clear this is a game that knows how to keep you hooked. It is smooth, polished, and easy to enjoy, but the longer you play, the more certain cracks start to show beneath the surface. Pros Visually Impressive World Mexico looks stunning. The environments are varied, from deserts and jungles to coastlines, and everything is detailed and well crafted. From a visual standpoint, it is hard to complain. Driving Feels Just Right The handling is where the game really shines. It is accessible without being boring, and whether you are racing seriously or just cruising, it feels consistently good. Massive Car Collection There is a huge range of vehicles to choose from. You are never really short on options, and experimenting with different builds keeps things interesting. Freedom in Gameplay You are not forced into anything. You can race, explore, tune, or just drive around. That flexibility makes it easy to pick up anytime. Long Lasting Appeal Even after 134 hours, it still has moments that pull you back in. The core gameplay loop is strong enough to hold attention over time. Cons World Feels Empty Over Time While the map looks beautiful, it can start to feel lifeless. Outside of events, there is not much happening dynamically, which makes long drives feel a bit hollow after a while. Repetitive Event Structure Many races and challenges start blending into each other. You notice the repetition more the longer you play. Weak Story Presence The story is minimal and forgettable. It does not add much to the overall experience. Online Inconsistencies Multiplayer is not always reliable. Connection issues and matchmaking problems can take away from the experience. AI Balance Issues The AI can feel uneven, either too easy or oddly difficult at times. Underwhelming Engine Sounds A noticeable drawback. Many cars lack distinct, powerful sound profiles, which takes away from the immersion, especially for a car focused game. Final Verdict Forza Horizon 5 gets the fundamentals right, driving, visuals, and accessibility, but it does not always maintain depth in the long run. It is a great game to jump into, but over time, the emptiness of the world and repetition start to stand out. Still, if you enjoy open world racing, it is worth experiencing.

Artistically handcrafted, narratively engaging, and [b]addictively replayable[/b], Hades expertly demonstrates just how well-made an action roguelite can be through [b]exceptional quality[/b]. Despite the mythological concepts introduced being simplified, these adjustments are better suited here. An energetically action-focused, rewarding gameplay loop ties these aspects together, but the [b]longevity of new content[/b] in challenges, progression, and additional details keeps this experience fresh long into your playthrough. A must-play game for the genre.

Titanfall 2 is one of the most underrated shooters of the last decade, delivering an exceptional blend of fast-paced action and a surprisingly emotional single-player campaign. The campaign is the game’s biggest surprise. You play as Jack Cooper, a rifleman who forms a bond with BT-7274, a Vanguard-class Titan. What starts as a straightforward sci-fi shooter evolves into a clever, varied experience filled with standout level design. Missions constantly introduce new mechanics such as time-shifting between past and present or gravity-defying platforming that keep gameplay fresh and inventive. The relationship between Cooper and BT adds genuine heart, making the story far more memorable than most FPS campaigns. Gameplay is where Titanfall 2 truly shines. The movement system—wall-running, sliding, double-jumping feels incredibly fluid and rewarding, encouraging speed and creativity rather than slow, cover-based combat. Pilots and Titans are both satisfying to control, and switching between agile infantry combat and the raw power of Titans creates an exciting rhythm that few shooters can match. Visually, the game still holds up well, with detailed environments, strong art direction, and smooth performance. The soundtrack complements the action perfectly, enhancing both the epic scale of Titan battles and the quieter character moments. A fantastic shooter on the Steam Deck and one of the best FPS games you can play....

I don’t usually write long reviews for games, but Titanfall 2 honestly deserves it. It’s one of those rare games that surprised me in the best possible way. I picked it up expecting a fun shooter, but what I got was a game with an amazing campaign, incredibly smooth gameplay, and one of the most enjoyable multiplayer experiences I’ve had in years. The single-player story is much better than I expected from a shooter like this. You play as Jack Cooper, a rifleman who ends up bonding with a Titan named BT-7274 after his commander dies in battle. What starts as a simple military mission slowly turns into a really emotional journey between a pilot and his Titan. BT isn’t just a machine that you call into battle - he actually feels like a real companion. Throughout the campaign you build a connection with him through dialogue, teamwork, and the situations you go through together. Some moments in the story are surprisingly touching, and by the end of the campaign I was way more invested than I expected. The missions themselves are incredibly creative. Instead of repeating the same shooting gallery over and over again, the game constantly introduces new mechanics. One level has you switching between two timelines in the middle of combat, another takes place in a factory that literally assembles entire buildings while you fight through it. It keeps the campaign feeling fresh the whole time, and I never felt bored or like I was just doing the same thing again and again. The gameplay is where Titanfall 2 really shines. The movement system is fantastic. Running on walls, sliding across the ground, jumping between rooftops, and chaining all those moves together feels incredibly smooth and natural. Once you get the hang of it, you feel almost unstoppable flying across the map. It’s one of those games where simply moving around is fun by itself. And then there are the Titans. Calling down a giant mech in the middle of a battle never gets old. Each Titan has its own abilities and weapons, which makes them feel very different from each other. Some are built for heavy damage, others are more tactical, and learning how to use them properly adds another layer of strategy to the game. The multiplayer is just as impressive. It’s fast, chaotic, and incredibly satisfying once you learn the movement system. Unlike many shooters where players move slowly and fights happen around corners, Titanfall 2 encourages constant motion. Players are running across walls, jumping across buildings, and dropping Titans onto the battlefield. It creates these huge, cinematic battles that feel unlike anything else. What I also like about the multiplayer is that it stays accessible. Even if you’re not the best player in the lobby, you can still contribute by fighting AI enemies, helping your team earn points, and working toward calling down your Titan. That makes the matches feel exciting even when you’re still learning the game. Visually, the game still looks great even years after release. The environments are detailed, the Titan designs are fantastic, and the animations are incredibly smooth. The sound design is also excellent - the heavy footsteps of Titans, the roar of weapons, and the music during intense battles all add a lot to the atmosphere. Overall, Titanfall 2 is easily one of the most underrated shooters ever made. The campaign is creative and emotional, the gameplay is incredibly smooth, and the multiplayer is both intense and fun. It’s the kind of game that reminds you why shooters can still be exciting when developers try something different. If you enjoy fast-paced action, great movement mechanics, and a surprisingly strong story, Titanfall 2 is absolutely worth playing. It’s a game that I still come back to, and every time I do, it reminds me just how special it is.

There’s a lot to say about this game’s launch and subsequent redemption, but from someone who played it through multiple endings before 2.0, most of the best parts of the game were always there, if not just more accessible now. The story is great, tense and complex with interesting characters that pulls you along all the while you as V build your rep by taking on fun, if not short, gigs throughout Night City. There’s some tastes of meaningful choice in the main story (and moreso in the DLC) but outside of that there’s little room for you to actually express yourself in this world, especially with how predetermined some aspects of your character are. Even basic features of expression like clothing, looks, and vehicles are seriously limited by a lot of modern RPG standards. More than that, one playthrough of the game’s main narratives will lead you through most of the game’s side content, with about 5 non-repeatable hours of “postgame content” (exclusively in the DLC). Sure, there’s always the other endings, but after that what are you left with? With how full Night City is I’m shocked by how dead the moment to moment exploration is. Night City is crowded, but hardly alive. It may be heretical to say, but outside of CD Projekt’s incredible curated content the transitory gameplay could be swapped with Starfield’s exploration. Its still well worth the money, ESPECIALLY recommended on sale, and mods can fill some of that empty space I’m dissatisfied with, but every so often I’ll stare wistfully at its icon before jumping in just to look at a cleared map and log out.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best games ever made. The story is truly unique and you really feel for the characters. The voice actors did a fantastic job especially male V. While some prefer the female performance, I found the male voice to be incredibly intimidating and impactful. The gameplay is top-notch. You can play differently every single run, and even repeating a build never feels boring. However, even with the freedom of the skill tree, some dialogue options or outcomes are blocked by the level cap. Even with mods, you can’t max out everything, which is one of the game's few downsides. Night City feels unique. Even without the random world events found in games like Red Dead Redemption 2, the side gigs provide plenty of content, offering at least 40 hours of playtime on a first run. The endings are also stellar; each one is distinct and worth experiencing. The romance options feel genuine because they require significant investment unlike The Witcher 3, where some encounters feel more random. Furthermore, the Phantom Liberty DLC improves on the base game's missions significantly. It’s clear CDPR wanted to create the best expansion possible. If you have a decent rig, this game is absolutely worth buying. It remains one of the best-looking titles on the market and a staple for hardware benchmarks. 10/10

[h3]TL;DR: Worth buying[/h3] I loved how the rougelike gameplay loop is tied to the story and how everything is connected, the story is decent, gameplay and atmosphere are great. But, you can say the same thing about every rougelike game.

This is the best game I've ever played. The gameplay loop is seamless, so that each failure or victory moves into the next. And it allows the player to continue to play after finishing the main story in a way that feels organic. It's also challenging without being overly difficult. It will take time to get good at, but the story is still unfolding even as you fail. Failure is an essential part of the experience. And the art and music are both some of the best I've ever heard/seen. I have more to say, but this is already long enough. TLDR; If you're even [b] considering [/b] buying Hades, do it. It's worth every penny and more. 10/10

This is my first Souls-like game, so I’m leaving comments open in case someone wants to share their perspective or maybe spark my interest in the genre again. That said, I genuinely don’t see the appeal. I played fairly deep into the game, far enough to defeat major bosses, slay something massive, and set something important on fire (no spoilers). So this isn’t a surface level take. Story: There barely is a story. What’s there feels vague and disconnected, more like a sequence of boss fights than a narrative. Lore exists, sure, but it’s buried so deeply that it never felt engaging or motivating to me. I never felt invested in what I was doing or why. Is it the genre? Like racing games where lore and story is not the point? Combat: It’s… fine. Rarely exciting. The biggest issue is rewards: you’re showered with an overwhelming number of weapons, most of which feel completely pointless. Beating around 95% of bosses gives you nothing meaningful, which is a big problem when the game is essentially a boss-rush experience. Progress often feels hollow. Setting: The world is technically open, but it feels lifeless. There are almost no people, no real villages, no towns just ruins and enemies. Exploration didn’t feel rewarding or immersive, it felt empty. An open world should invite curiosity, not make you feel alone in a dead museum. Overall I don’t understand the obsession. For me, Elden Ring feels more like endurance than enjoyment and I will not be returning to the genre again... Maybe for that Napoleon era game.

Overall Score: 6/10 - The gameplay is engaging and fun, especially with friends. However the problem lies within its half-baked story, bland environment and locked content. Gameplay: 4/5 - The gameplay is quite fun! It feels very intuitive and easy to pick up. Allowing you to play on both controller and wheel. Story: 0/5 - Unfortunately the story feels pretty uninspired, the characters lack much depth and the entire plot doesn't serve much purpose to the game as a whole. Obviously it's not a major part of the game, but it's still apart of it regardless. But easily the worst part about it, is a lack of skipable cutscenes. You have to watch every single one in full, which can get a bit annoying after some time. I'd rather just drive my cars and not be apart of the cutscenes entirely. Difficulty: 2/5 - At first it may be difficult learning how the car reacts to the road, especially if your new to racing games. But fairly quickly you'll get the hang of it without much trouble. Progression: 2/5 - You can get tons of cars for just playing. However some cars are locked behind either DLC, or weekly challenges. Forcing your players into weekly challenges just to unlock certain cars feels pretty bad. Not to mention if there is a specific car you want, you have to pray it comes back, without guarantee it ever will. Replay Value: 3/5 - Single player gets a bit stale. Community: 5/5 - Friendly and not toxic. Graphics: 3/5 - It looks good, but the environment isn't very captivating. Audio: 3/5 - Cars sound nice. The soundtrack isn't particularly astounding. Price: 1/5 - Buy on sale. Conclusion: Do I think FH5 is worth it? That depends on what you want in a racing game. If you want a fun and engaging community with solid gameplay to support it. Then this game is perfect! If you would like to collect every car and be a completionist, then please know it's not really possible in its current state. But that's okay! Because at its core it's a fun game. And that's enough for most people.

Forza Horizon 5 is a game that impresses from the very first moments. What stands out the most is the excellent graphic quality - the world of Mexico is brought to life with incredible attention to detail. The landscapes are vibrant, diverse, and full of depth, making every drive across the map truly satisfying. The lighting, weather effects, and overall visual design are all top-tier. The soundtrack fits the atmosphere of the game flawlessly — it boosts the excitement during races and enhances the festival vibe during calmer moments. I was also very positively surprised by the story, which this time is more engaging, richer, and better executed than in the previous entries. The narrative draws you into the world of racing and Mexican culture in a smooth and enjoyable way. The only thing I felt was missing is that cars had slightly more detailed models in FH 4 It’s a small remark, but fans of automotive realism might notice it. Despite this minor drawback, FH 5 is a fantastic game that I can wholeheartedly recommend — beautiful, dynamic, polished, and full of great energy. It’s perfect for both newcomers and long-time fans of the series.

It is really mind blowing the amount of car variety if you come from a sane/grounded perspective. The bad part of this game is the damn story. It is awful. The writing, the pace, the dialog. Refer to what Microsoft was up to during this title release. The great part is the map, racing, roads, graphics. The game is gorgeous. Although missing seasons like H4 with snow, it is a great experience having the feel of change on the weather when seasons changes. After getting rid of the compulsory story you can have the freedom to do what you want, race where you want on the map, which features long stretch of roads and higher speeds than H4. It is a great time sink for 15 minutes to 2h~ as it has great drifting gameplay that's quite satisfying. A powerful photomode is there for who likes to make art out of games. Car customisation lacks a lot. Internal upgrades are better than H4 but yet not quite there imo. Still nice to engine swap an 80s ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ into a monster. Nice is an understatement. I like it. A bit large on storage. Compulsory login into Xbox. I don't have an issue with neither, but beware.

The first 50 or so hours are enjoyable, however after you collect most of the cars, the game slows down and the grind for backstage passes kills it for me. Don't get me wrong, I think the idea of doing challenges for cars or items is cool, but the grind is too much and after doing it two or three times. The grind only seems to be there not to reward the player, but to incentivize the player to make another purchase. The map, while visually impressive, is too spaced out and not dense enough to make it fun. The roads are too wide and do not convey a sense of speed very well (something Forza 4 was very strong in). The size of the map is great, but I just wish it was more dense, so you really have a lot more to explore. Lastly, the voice acting and writing in the game is one of its largest shortfalls. The writing for the in-game characters is flat and stale. They use this really cheesy spanglish that comes off as tacky and is often annoying. At points it sounds like a children's game, with unnatural speech. This game had the potential to be the best in the series, but unfortunately does not hold a candle to Forza 3 and 4. Especially in the contents that keeps people hooked, which an open-world game like this deserves.

Hades is one of those games that need no introduction, it has claimed it's place in history as the best rouge-lites ever made, and whilst I don't know if it ranks that highly on my list purely as a rouge-lite, it does place highly as just a fantastic, well made game that everyone should try, this is the perfect gateway into the genre and has already introduced millions. What Hades does better than games like slay the spire, risk of rain and dead cells is that it puts narrative at the forefront, with an incredible ensemble of characters that are memorable with excellent voice acting and an eye watering amount of dialogue. Hades succeeds in pulling in even people who don't play rouge-lites due to the way it handles death, even if you die in the first room multiple times it's likely characters will have new dialogue. The game takes the edge of death and makes it less of a punishment and more a narrative tool. So how's gameplay? Well very good to be blunt. In essence this game is similar to diablo, in which it's a top down rpg in which you hack and slash your way through various dungeons all with greek mythology serving as the backdrop. You pick powers from different gods, using a variety of interesting weapons and fight hordes of enemies only to die and do it all again. Combat is incredibly fast and fluid with the build variety being quite staggering. The more you play the more the game hands out new systems which keeps the repetitive nature of the game fresh. Story, music, presentation are all top quality. As mentioned the amount of dialogue is insane but it would mean nothing if the voice acting sucked or if the story was uninteresting. Thankfully this is a game that delivers on all fronts, characters are memorable, the main character zagreus is enduring and the titular Hades is intimidating. I think my only issue is the fact that some areas and bosses do get quite samey and build variety whilst varied does start falling into the meta trap when you just want to start smashing out clears. For pure rouge-lite I'd always lean towards dead cells but for the simple experience of a good game, hades is unmatched. In short Hades is fantastic, that one of a kind game that has bridged the gap for a genre that was quite niche and brought it into the mainstream, hades has been an incredible gane bringing in many to the genre and has gone on to show the narrative power only games can achieve.

Hades is a roguelite action game built around Zagreus, the son of Hades, as he repeatedly attempts to escape the Underworld. On paper, it follows a familiar run-based structure, but what makes it exceptional is how every failed escape feels meaningful. Instead of treating death as a reset, the game turns it into progression, storytelling, character development, and motivation to try again. The combat is fast, responsive, and endlessly satisfying. Each weapon feels distinct, and the Boons from Olympian gods constantly reshape how a run plays out. One attempt might revolve around lightning-fast melee aggression, while another becomes a ranged build focused on poison, deflection, or critical damage. The game encourages experimentation without making failure feel punishing, and its balance is strong enough that almost every build can become viable with the right choices. What truly elevates Hades is how seamlessly it blends gameplay and narrative. Characters remember your attempts, comment on your progress, and evolve over time through conversations, gifts, and side stories. The writing is sharp, funny, emotional, and remarkably consistent. Even after dozens of runs, there is still new dialogue to uncover, which makes the Underworld feel alive rather than repetitive. Progression is excellent. Permanent upgrades, weapon aspects, keepsakes, house renovations, and relationship systems all give you reasons to keep playing beyond simply reaching the surface. The game constantly rewards effort in small but meaningful ways, creating one of the most addictive loops in the genre. Even when a run goes badly, you usually come away with resources, knowledge, or new story moments. The presentation is outstanding. The art style is bold and expressive, the soundtrack is incredible, and the voice acting gives every character personality. From the House of Hades to the chaos of combat, every part of the game feels polished and intentional. It is stylish without sacrificing readability, which is especially important in such a fast-paced game. There are very few real weaknesses. Some late-game progression can become grindy, especially when chasing specific upgrades or story resolutions, and repeated areas naturally lose a little surprise over time. But these are minor issues in a game that remains engaging far longer than most roguelites. [hr][/hr] [b]Highlights:[/b] [list] [*]Fast, precise, and highly satisfying combat [*]Excellent weapon variety and build experimentation [*]Brilliant integration of roguelite structure and storytelling [*]Memorable characters with consistently strong writing [*]Rewarding progression that makes every run feel worthwhile [*]Outstanding art direction, music, and voice acting [*]Late-game progression can become slightly grindy [/list] [hr][/hr] [b]TL;DR:[/b] Hades is a near-perfect roguelite that combines sharp combat, meaningful progression, and exceptional storytelling into one of the most polished games in the genre. Every failed run still feels rewarding, every character adds personality, and every system works together to keep the experience fresh, addictive, and memorable.
The amount of effort and love put into this gem are ostensively weaved into every corners of it. Truly, a memorable piece that stands out in the annals of the classics.

[u]An absolute must‑play within the FromSoftware lineage.[/u] Elden Ring takes the studio’s signature challenge‑driven design and expands it into a sweeping open world that feels endlessly explorable. While it departs from the tightly structured progression of Dark Souls 1–3 (a format I personally prefer) the shift still brings a unique strength. The Lands Between evoke the same sense of boundless possibility that made Skyrim so iconic, rewarding curiosity with challenging encounters, layered storytelling, and a level of discovery rarely matched in modern RPGs. However, this sense of discovery didn't come without drawbacks. The sheer freedom of pathing makes FromSoftware’s already cryptic questlines even harder to track, often to the point of feeling overwhelming. NPC arcs can become fragmented or unintentionally skipped, and the open structure occasionally disrupts the narrative flow, creating moments where major story beats feel out of order or disconnected from the intended progression. Regarding the graphics, it’s impossible not to highlight the sheer beauty of the world FromSoftware has crafted. Every vista, dungeon, and battlefield feels meticulously composed, often looking more like art then the video games of past. Whether standing still to admire the horizon or caught in the chaos of combat, nearly every moment feels screenshot-worthy. It’s a visually astonishing experience that elevates the sense of wonder throughout the journey.

Elden Ring stands as a seminal achievement in interactive myth-making. One thing this game does is encourage an approach to character progression. Whether you prefer the visceral, heavy-hitting cadence of a colossal sword or the distance of glintstone sorceries, the mechanical framework is amazing. The game really shines when you start experimenting with making hybrid builds, like mixing stats like Strength and Faith or Dexterity and Arcane to create a build that feels entirely personal. The lore is this game is really mind-blowing as it doesn't just hand you a plot, it sort of force you to piece together a tragic mystery of a broken world. As a "tarnished" which is sent into the world long after signifcant events occur, witnessing the aftermath of a war that fractured reality itself and creating a narrative depth it make the game feel both haunting and monumental. A game that truly earns its title of GOTY and will undoubtedly remain a cherished masterpiece for many.

Titanfall 2 is a fast, stylish shooter about parkour, giant robots, and does something rare: it tells a complete, memorable story in a tight package. There’s no bloated open world. No checklist obsession. No cinematic excess. Just clever level design, strong pacing, and one time-manipulation level that casually reminds the industry what creativity looks like. And then it emotionally blindsides you with a war machine who understands sacrifice better than the humans around him . BT is a Titan. He is programmed for combat, tactics, and survival. He speaks in calm, precise statements. He does not joke. He does not hesitate. And yet somehow, he is the most emotionally intelligent character in the entire game. BT listens. BT trusts you. He doesn’t say “I care.” He says, “Protocol 3: Protect the Pilot.” And somehow that hits harder. The art style does the heavy lifting. Strong silhouettes, bold colors, and readable environments make the game look sharp without needing ultra-realistic textures. The movement is incredible, wall-running, sliding, double-jumping - it’s pure momentum-driven joy. Combat on foot feels sharp and skillful. Calling down your Titan feels powerful every single time. Vince Zampella didn’t chase trends. He set standards. A timeless shooter, still ahead of its time.

Titanfall 2 feels like a masterclass in single player first-person shooter design and is well-optimized delivering a great visual experience on modest hardware. On the Lenovo Legion Go S (Z1 Extreme), the game runs beautifully, achieving 60 FPS usually at 1080p. The graphics design is nothing short of awesome, featuring striking industrial aesthetics and vibrant alien landscapes. The gameplay is exceptionally varied, seamlessly transitioning between fluid, high-speed parkour as a Pilot and the heavy, tactical power-fantasy of piloting a Titan. The campaign’s cinematic presentation is incredibly entertaining, utilizing creative level design and a genuine bond between the protagonist and his mech to drive the narrative forward. Crucially, the experience is tightly paced and does not overstay its welcome. The only significant hurdle is the mandatory EA Launcher; its inclusion adds a cumbersome layer of complexity that requires linking an EA account and can occasionally lead to launch errors. Despite this administrative friction, the game itself is an absolute gem that shines brightly on handheld hardware. I did not play the multiplayer component.

Titanfall 2 is an outstanding FPS with one of the best single-player stories in the genre. Combining a strong narrative with fast, fluid shooting is a genius idea, and it’s executed beautifully. It’s easily one of the best FPS games ever made and helped Apex Legends come into fruition. The multiplayer, however, is not the best, long queue times depending on servers and the usual cheaters. It never matched the story’s quality.

Verdict: One of the most mechanically refined shooters ever made, with a campaign that still sets the bar for FPS design. Titanfall 2’s greatest strength is how fluidly it blends movement, gunplay, and verticality. Wall-running, sliding, and grappling are not gimmicks—they are fundamental to how combat flows. The result is a shooter where positioning and momentum matter as much as aim. The single-player campaign deserves special mention. Each level introduces a new mechanic and fully explores it before moving on, avoiding repetition while constantly teaching the player something new. The relationship between pilot and Titan is handled with surprising emotional weight, elevating the narrative beyond typical FPS storytelling. Multiplayer remains fast, skill-based, and rewarding, though the player base can feel uneven at times due to matchmaking population swings. Still, when matches click, few shooters offer the same sense of kinetic satisfaction. What Works Well Exceptional movement mechanics One of the best FPS campaigns ever made Clear visual and mechanical readability High skill ceiling without feeling unfair What Needs Improvement Multiplayer population inconsistency Limited long-term content support Final Thoughts: Titanfall 2 is a masterclass in FPS design. It may not have the ongoing support of newer titles, but its core gameplay remains unmatched.

After spending about 120 hours in Forza Horizon 5 and unlocking almost all of the achievements, I feel like I have experienced nearly everything the game has to offer. First of all, the game is visually stunning. The map based on Mexico is beautiful, the car selection is huge, and the driving physics are still some of the best in the arcade-racing genre. However, after a long time playing, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive. Many events begin to feel the same, and this is something that also reminds me of Forza Horizon 4. The core gameplay loop hasn’t changed much between the two games. The DLCs are a mixed experience. The Rally Adventure DLC is actually quite interesting. The rally mechanics, dirt roads, and more technical driving create a refreshing change of pace compared to the base game. It feels more focused and challenging, which I appreciated. On the other hand, the Hot Wheels DLC was less interesting for me. While the tracks look impressive and creative, the gameplay quickly becomes more about spectacle than driving skill, and the novelty wears off faster than expected. One mode that I personally didn’t enjoy is “The Eliminator”. While the idea of a battle-royale style racing mode is creative, in practice it often feels frustrating and somewhat random. Encounters can depend too much on luck, car drops, or map positioning rather than pure driving skill. Because of this, the mode never really felt satisfying or balanced to me, even though I appreciate the attempt to add something different. Another downside is the lack of a meaningful story. There are some narrative elements, but they are very light and mostly serve as short introductions to events. Compared to how big the game world is, the story content feels minimal. Overall, Forza Horizon 5 is still a very polished and enjoyable racing game, especially in the first dozens of hours. But after completing most of the achievements and spending over 120 hours in the game, the repetition and lack of deeper progression or story can make it feel a bit monotonous. Still, for fans of arcade racing and car collecting, it remains a solid experience.

review_text: Forza Horizon 5 feels like a [b]tech demo[/b]. [h2]the core and technical aspects[/h2] the core of the game - driving and racing the cars - is incredibly well done and has clearly had a lot of effort and time invested towards it over the course of the franchise's lifespan. the simcade engine is the best of its kind and no other competitor comes close. driving remains immensely satisfying irrespective of the type of vehicle you're maneuvering, the terrain surface you're on, or weather conditions you're under. the game consistently looks, sounds, and performs very well. [hr][/hr] but it ends there. it's as if the developers had invested a lot of time and care into creating an incredibly solid base for a racing game, but then skimped out on all the additional aspects that wouldn't have required nearly as much effort or resources, but that would've greatly contributed to the quality of the final product. that's where the tech demo analogy comes from. first case in point: [h2]the map[/h2] the team was clearly capable of creating a large, varied, beautiful, and functional open world map. Mexico certainly ticks all of those boxes, and more: the volcano, the jungles, the many long, winding and twisting roads with great verticality, the beach town, the stadium and test track - i could go on. [b]on paper it's perfect[/b]. i much prefer it to the predecessor's Edinburgh. but holy sh*t is it [b]empty[/b]. the NPC vehicle traffic is so incredibly sparse. there are [i]zero[/i] pedestrians, like, at all. there's no people. there's no proper intersections, no parking garages, no gas stations, no traffic lights. there's no [i]things happening[/i]. no airplanes in the sky, boats on water, no service vehicles, no wildlife (outside of howler monkeys? and some birds), no events. the one urban area in the game feels like a complete ghost town. it's embarrassing. it looks and feels completely fake. this has been the case throughout the entirety of the franchise's lifespan. The Crew perfected the open-world racing map in 2018. so why can't Forza Horizon? [h2]story[/h2] terrible and completely dispensable in every possible aspect. ninety five percent of the storylines revolve around you driving a vehicle from point A to point B on the map while some at best completely forgettable and at worst extremely annoying character yaps about some boring ♥♥♥♥ in an irritatingly fake and forced spanish accent with involuntary spansih lingo sprinkled in occasionally. it's all totally dry, inoffensive, and boring, with zero character, no emotion, and a total lack of any plot. just absolutely terrible. the only slightly redeemable aspect are some of the scripted "Showcase" events, which seem more like technical presentations rather than parts of the story. [h2]progression[/h2] there is none. the currency model is optimized... - for the 10 year old playing the game on the living room Xbox whose parents bought it for him at $80, and who certainly wouldn't appreciate driving a beat-down Ford for the first 10 hours of the game. and that's fine. but there has to be a fine line, a compromise? the game showers you with rewards at every possible step. you earn credits as a reward for completing races, showcases, and events - and cars (and their upgrades) [i]do[/i] cost credits - but that aspect very quickly becomes totally irrelevant as you're constantly rewarded with Wheelspins, which in turn give you credits and cars in extreme abundance. the new "Accolades" system is a diamond in the rough - a good idea in isolation, which ultimately suffers from being part of a larger, flawed system. the one aspect of progression that's done right is what the game aptly calls [i]Hard To Find[/i] cars - ones that cannot be purchased outright using credits nor won in a wheelspin. instead, they appear for limited time in either the [i]Forzathon Shop[/i] or as a reward in a seasonal Festival Playlist. and it is this limited nature and the FOMO associated with it is what makes you want to play the game and acquire the car, and what ultimately makes it that much more satisfying once you do. -- but even so it's hard to make these cars appear special or unique next to their cheap, readily available 150,000 CR supercar counterparts. so - if there's no story to follow or get invested into, and little feeling of progression as you play - what's left? [hr][/hr] well, it's not all bleak. again, the activities that benefit most from the game's great foundation are thankfully the ones you'll spend most of your time on - racing (whether against AI or online versus real opponents) and simply cruising around the map. and they're very polished, really enjoyable, and in my opinion enough to just barely overshadow all the negatives. at its core, Forza Horizon 5 is still very enjoyable. it just sucks that i can't help but keep wondering just how much better it would've been with a bit more effort.

review_text: Overview After 134 hours with Forza Horizon 5, it is clear this is a game that knows how to keep you hooked. It is smooth, polished, and easy to enjoy, but the longer you play, the more certain cracks start to show beneath the surface. Pros Visually Impressive World Mexico looks stunning. The environments are varied, from deserts and jungles to coastlines, and everything is detailed and well crafted. From a visual standpoint, it is hard to complain. Driving Feels Just Right The handling is where the game really shines. It is accessible without being boring, and whether you are racing seriously or just cruising, it feels consistently good. Massive Car Collection There is a huge range of vehicles to choose from. You are never really short on options, and experimenting with different builds keeps things interesting. Freedom in Gameplay You are not forced into anything. You can race, explore, tune, or just drive around. That flexibility makes it easy to pick up anytime. Long Lasting Appeal Even after 134 hours, it still has moments that pull you back in. The core gameplay loop is strong enough to hold attention over time. Cons World Feels Empty Over Time While the map looks beautiful, it can start to feel lifeless. Outside of events, there is not much happening dynamically, which makes long drives feel a bit hollow after a while. Repetitive Event Structure Many races and challenges start blending into each other. You notice the repetition more the longer you play. Weak Story Presence The story is minimal and forgettable. It does not add much to the overall experience. Online Inconsistencies Multiplayer is not always reliable. Connection issues and matchmaking problems can take away from the experience. AI Balance Issues The AI can feel uneven, either too easy or oddly difficult at times. Underwhelming Engine Sounds A noticeable drawback. Many cars lack distinct, powerful sound profiles, which takes away from the immersion, especially for a car focused game. Final Verdict Forza Horizon 5 gets the fundamentals right, driving, visuals, and accessibility, but it does not always maintain depth in the long run. It is a great game to jump into, but over time, the emptiness of the world and repetition start to stand out. Still, if you enjoy open world racing, it is worth experiencing.

Hades is a roguelite action game built around Zagreus, the son of Hades, as he repeatedly attempts to escape the Underworld. On paper, it follows a familiar run-based structure, but what makes it exceptional is how every failed escape feels meaningful. Instead of treating death as a reset, the game turns it into progression, storytelling, character development, and motivation to try again. The combat is fast, responsive, and endlessly satisfying. Each weapon feels distinct, and the Boons from Olympian gods constantly reshape how a run plays out. One attempt might revolve around lightning-fast melee aggression, while another becomes a ranged build focused on poison, deflection, or critical damage. The game encourages experimentation without making failure feel punishing, and its balance is strong enough that almost every build can become viable with the right choices. What truly elevates Hades is how seamlessly it blends gameplay and narrative. Characters remember your attempts, comment on your progress, and evolve over time through conversations, gifts, and side stories. The writing is sharp, funny, emotional, and remarkably consistent. Even after dozens of runs, there is still new dialogue to uncover, which makes the Underworld feel alive rather than repetitive. Progression is excellent. Permanent upgrades, weapon aspects, keepsakes, house renovations, and relationship systems all give you reasons to keep playing beyond simply reaching the surface. The game constantly rewards effort in small but meaningful ways, creating one of the most addictive loops in the genre. Even when a run goes badly, you usually come away with resources, knowledge, or new story moments. The presentation is outstanding. The art style is bold and expressive, the soundtrack is incredible, and the voice acting gives every character personality. From the House of Hades to the chaos of combat, every part of the game feels polished and intentional. It is stylish without sacrificing readability, which is especially important in such a fast-paced game. There are very few real weaknesses. Some late-game progression can become grindy, especially when chasing specific upgrades or story resolutions, and repeated areas naturally lose a little surprise over time. But these are minor issues in a game that remains engaging far longer than most roguelites. [hr][/hr] [b]Highlights:[/b] [list] [*]Fast, precise, and highly satisfying combat [*]Excellent weapon variety and build experimentation [*]Brilliant integration of roguelite structure and storytelling [*]Memorable characters with consistently strong writing [*]Rewarding progression that makes every run feel worthwhile [*]Outstanding art direction, music, and voice acting [*]Late-game progression can become slightly grindy [/list] [hr][/hr] [b]TL;DR:[/b] Hades is a near-perfect roguelite that combines sharp combat, meaningful progression, and exceptional storytelling into one of the most polished games in the genre. Every failed run still feels rewarding, every character adds personality, and every system works together to keep the experience fresh, addictive, and memorable.

Do you like big, open-world games and bleak, dystopian science fiction films? Do you like good storylines where decisions affect the outcomes? If you value your job and/or family time, you may want to set the alarm on your phone to drag you back into the real world every now and then. I played this on a Windows PC using an Xbox controller and that worked fine, although the controls could sometimes be a little fiddly. Elden Ring is a massive achievement, but the difficulty sometimes feels like its coming from the wrong place. After putting in over 100 hours, I have a few thoughts. The Good: World & Play The level design is genuinely amazing. The way the world is built is top-tier; these levels are expansive, twisting, and turning into each other in ways that are actually hard to wrap your head around. It’s beautiful to look at, and the enemy variety is awesome. The 'come up' of getting stronger is where it really shines. The Bad: Controls & "Artificial" Difficulty I found the controls to be ridiculous, I don't think making a game harder with cumbersome controls is good design. The queue up system for inputs acts so strange that I found myself still making mistakes even after 100+ hours. The amount of times I have accidently dismounted from my horse its unbelievable, call me bad, but this is my experience. Bad physics isn't a puzzle, it's just frustrating. Same goes for some of the site of grace layouts; tedious for no real gain. The Ugly: Narrative & Inventory The story makes very little sense. Call me a smooth brain, but FromSoft just doesn't tell a good story I almost never knew what I was actually doing.. The lack of explanation carries over to items, I have a million things in my inventory, most of which where useless, or that I had no idea how to use. Managing it all was a chore; when the expansion started I had to look up what the first item did. Why? Multiplayer: PVP & Coop The PVP was mostly try hards wasting my time, the native coop is quite clucky and I highly recommend Seamless Co-op mod, it made the experience a lot better for me. It removes a ton of the friction from cooperative play. Performance: My PC is a literal god computer, and I’m still seeing 40 FPS at times. Lul. Final Take: Its a gorgeous, expansive world with fun boss fights, and great multiplayer held back by clunky UI and controls. I still recommend it, its a fun game, but its probably going to piss you off at times.

Elden Ring is a massive achievement, but the difficulty sometimes feels like its coming from the wrong place. After putting in over 100 hours, I have a few thoughts. The Good: World & Play The level design is genuinely amazing. The way the world is built is top-tier; these levels are expansive, twisting, and turning into each other in ways that are actually hard to wrap your head around. It’s beautiful to look at, and the enemy variety is awesome. The 'come up' of getting stronger is where it really shines. The Bad: Controls & "Artificial" Difficulty I found the controls to be ridiculous, I don't think making a game harder with cumbersome controls is good design. The queue up system for inputs acts so strange that I found myself still making mistakes even after 100+ hours. The amount of times I have accidently dismounted from my horse its unbelievable, call me bad, but this is my experience. Bad physics isn't a puzzle, it's just frustrating. Same goes for some of the site of grace layouts; tedious for no real gain. The Ugly: Narrative & Inventory The story makes very little sense. Call me a smooth brain, but FromSoft just doesn't tell a good story I almost never knew what I was actually doing.. The lack of explanation carries over to items, I have a million things in my inventory, most of which where useless, or that I had no idea how to use. Managing it all was a chore; when the expansion started I had to look up what the first item did. Why? Multiplayer: PVP & Coop The PVP was mostly try hards wasting my time, the native coop is quite clucky and I highly recommend Seamless Co-op mod, it made the experience a lot better for me. It removes a ton of the friction from cooperative play. Performance: My PC is a literal god computer, and I’m still seeing 40 FPS at times. Lul. Final Take: Its a gorgeous, expansive world with fun boss fights, and great multiplayer held back by clunky UI and controls. I still recommend it, its a fun game, but its probably going to piss you off at times.
