review_text: This game is the absolute manifestation of perfection in gaming. As a fairly new player to the souls-like genre, I was worried initially. Not that I wouldn't like the game, I was rather worried about mechanical confusion. I was worried about the fact that I couldn't understand the game. This primarily stems from the fact that the lack of guidance can be problematic. That doesn't mean I want the game to literally take me by my hand and lead me to the ending, but complete lack of guidance makes the game less enjoyable for me. Elden Ring balances this perfectly. Yes, there were some things that required research, mainly new mechanics, but the guidance is firm and telling enough to give me breathing space. The game clearly tells you "go in that direction, and you will progress in some way", and then hints at what is optional. Its not written anywhere clearly, like in a quest log, but there are subtle and simple ways of guiding you that do not spoil you the game. Something that should also be noted is the method of storytelling. I had to learn this externally, but the game does not "tell a story" through collectibles, which is boring. The game tells a story by the environment. Almost everything in this game has a reason for its location, appearance, and behavior. Bosses tend resemble their personalities in the way they move, attack, speak, everything. The environment is shaped in such ways to tell a story. An NPC being concealed doesn't have to be just a visual decision, it can resemble something deeper and important. Not a lot of games take it to such a depth and often things looks the way "just because they were designed that way". A knight can have a very consistent pattern of attacking that does not change, because it literally "keeps calm". A teacher can test you, be consistent, and incredibly calm, but then once you fight his "real self", he throws away the composure, and becomes much more violent and desperate. The game does not have a perfectly linear gameplay, but it does not fail at "telling where is the main progress" either. if a fight feels too hard, you should come back later once you are stronger. Or you can switch up your strategy and lure the enemy somewhere. Weapons are not perfectly universal, and tend to have specific uses for specific situations. So holding onto one single weapon is not very ideal here, because experimenting is rewarded. A common complaint I see is the difficulty of this game. And I agree this game is difficult, but there is also a clear distinction between "difficult, because RNG", and "difficult, because of complex mechanics". there are games that are difficult only because of RNG, meaning you barely control the outcomes, the random elements do instead. These games tend to be much more frustrating, because you can learn only a very limited range of things, because there is so much outside of your control. But here? The game is not difficult, because of a ton of elements that you basically cannot control. The game is difficult, because of mechanical complexity. Bossfights, for example, are difficult, because you need to learn patterns. Learn patterns, recovery windows, read the enemy movement, tune your equipment,... Each death that happens has a clear reason. If you happen to die, you always know why and what killed you. The visual clarity is strong enough that you notice it and physically see it. This is the type of difficulty that is much less random and actually is fair. A boss can be extreme hard, but still can be extremely fun, even if you repeatedly die over and over. You never have to deal with the boss being extremely random and unpredictable. This is the closes to a skill-based game you can ever get. Yes, there are downsides. Especially in the engine. The game is obviously meant to be played with a controller, and on a console. That does not mean its unplayable on a keyboard, I would say the experience is pretty okay, but some keybinds can feel weird, and you may need to change them. The game is also permanently locked at 60fps, so your 1000hz monitor is useless here. And while unlocking it is possible, it can have some unpredictable outcomes, like some animations breaking, or acting weirdly. Not to mention that the engine is not really suited to hyper-optimize games. Foliage can be an issue, mainly around forests and trees. It can lower your fps on high settings, despite having capable hardware. I would also enjoy a bit better explanations of some systems. Not to necessarily add new explanations to gameplay mechanics, but to rather make the existing ones more clear and understandable. In the end I would say that the game is absolutely amazing. Its not often that I get so excited from games, and this one really made me enjoy gaming the same way when I was a young kid completely new to gaming. The price is a little high with small sales, but I would say its definitely worth it!

The characters and story give a soul to a game that already feels full of life. The music and art are endearing and complement the atmosphere very well. There is consistently more to the game than meets the eye. In addition to all of this, I think the main thing that made me keep playing was the sense of progression. No matter what my goal was at the time, it always felt like I was making progress. There's always a small, medium, and large goal to work toward. If any one of them begin to feel stale, you can shift your focus without moving backward. Advancing in any scope feels rewarding. From a more external perspective, it has an extensive and well-organized wiki. It has great mod support and plenty of tools and trackers to support unmodded gameplay. The updates never detract from the game, and if anything they feel natural and integrate very well into the existing content. The gameplay is smooth and the performance is good. It's worth the price and then some. Stardew Valley is so much more than a farming sim. Stardew is great if you like grinding. It's great if you like to play casually. It's fun if you like collecting, and satisfying if you're a completionist. It's structured if you like to plan things out, and flexible if you're a more free-form player. It's equally as good a singleplayer as it is a multiplayer game. There is not a single area in which it doesn't exceed my expectations.

​Stardew Valley is, at its core, a masterpiece of the cozy-farming genre. Whether you’re meticulously planning your crop rotations, delving into the mines, or wooing the local villagers, the game offers a level of charm and depth that is rarely matched. It shines brightest when played with a partner or friends—sharing the workload of a growing farm makes the experience feel truly collaborative and rewarding. ​The Breaking Point: "Connecting to Online Services..." However, the current technical state of the game has made it nearly impossible to recommend for those looking for that specific multiplayer magic. Recently, many players (myself included) have hit a literal brick wall: the co-op menu often hangs indefinitely on the message "connecting to online services." This isn't just a minor lag spike; it’s a total service failure that prevents the multiplayer menu from even loading, effectively stripping away the game’s best feature. While the single-player experience remains intact, the lack of a reliable fix for these server-side handshake issues makes the "Co-op" button feel like a decorative ornament rather than a functional feature.
